Gerard Debreu was a French‑American economist whose work reshaped modern general equilibrium theory. He was born in 1919 and earned his doctorate under the supervision of Paul Samuelson at MIT. In 1959 he published the landmark book Theory of Value: An Axiomatic Analysis of Economic Equilibrium. This work presented a rigorous mathematical foundation for the existence of competitive equilibria. Debreu combined the tools of convex analysis, topology, and fixed‑point theorems to prove that markets can reach a state where supply equals demand. His proof relied on the Kakutani fixed‑point theorem, extending the earlier work of Arrow and Hicks. By formulating preferences, technologies, and endowments as well‑behaved mathematical objects, he showed that an equilibrium exists under realistic assumptions. The model assumes a finite number of agents, each maximizing a continuous, strictly convex utility function. Production technologies are represented by convex, closed sets. Prices are taken as a vector in a positive orthant, normalized to avoid trivial solutions. Debreu’s theorem requires that excess demand functions be continuous and satisfy Walras’ law. The proof demonstrates that a price vector can be found where excess demand is zero for every commodity. This result gave formal justification to the notion of a market‑clearing price system. Debreu also introduced the concept of a “price system” as a complete set of commodity prices that coordinates all markets. His work clarified the role of price mechanisms in allocating resources efficiently. A central implication of Debreu’s equilibrium is the First Welfare Theorem. The theorem states that any competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient, meaning no individual can be made better off without making someone else worse off. This links the abstract notion of equilibrium to the normative idea of economic efficiency. Debreu’s analysis showed that under convexity and perfect competition, the market outcome cannot be improved upon by a planner. The Second Welfare Theorem, also derived from his framework, asserts that any Pareto efficient allocation can be supported as a competitive equilibrium given appropriate transfers of wealth. This highlights the potential for redistributive policies without sacrificing efficiency. Debreu’s contributions also formalized the conditions under which multiple equilibria can arise. He showed that if preferences or technologies are not strictly convex, the equilibrium may be non‑unique. This insight opened a research agenda on equilibrium selection and stability. His mathematical style emphasized axiomatic rigor, influencing subsequent generations of economists. The rigorous treatment helped embed general equilibrium theory into mainstream economic analysis. Debreu’s work inspired the development of computable general equilibrium (CGE) models used for policy simulation. These models apply his equilibrium conditions to large‑scale economies with many sectors and agents. The implications for welfare analysis are profound, as CGE models can assess how policy changes affect efficiency and distribution. Debreu’s theory also underpins modern financial economics, where asset markets are treated as part of a general equilibrium system. The concept of market completeness, central to modern finance, traces its formal roots to Debreu’s framework. Moreover, his approach clarified the role of assumptions such as perfect information and price taking behavior. When these assumptions fail, the efficiency results may break down, leading to market failures. Debreu’s rigorous proof of equilibrium existence provided a benchmark against which alternative market structures are evaluated. His work earned him the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1983, shared with Kenneth Arrow. The award recognized their joint contributions to general equilibrium and welfare economics. Debreu’s legacy extends beyond his published theorems; he mentored many prominent economists. His students continued to explore the boundaries of equilibrium theory. The impact of his work is evident in contemporary research on mechanism design, auction theory, and market design. By establishing a clear mathematical foundation, Debreu enabled economists to test the robustness of efficiency claims. In summary, Gerard Debreu’s contributions provided the first fully rigorous proof that competitive markets can reach an equilibrium. The resulting theorems connect market outcomes to Pareto efficiency, offering both explanatory and normative insights. His work shows that under ideal conditions, markets allocate resources optimally, but also highlights the fragile dependence on those conditions. Understanding Debreu’s theory helps economists assess when real‑world markets approximate the ideal and when intervention may be warranted. The educational value of his contributions lies in illustrating how precise mathematical assumptions translate into powerful economic conclusions.

Civilians in western Mosul are increasingly caught in the crossfire as Iraqi forces tighten their offensive against entrenched Islamic State fighters. Over the past week, the Iraqi army, supported by allied militia units and coalition air strikes, has launched a series of coordinated assaults aimed at reclaiming the densely populated districts that the group has held since 2014. Residents report that heavy artillery bombardments and air raids have shattered homes, schools and markets, prompting thousands to flee the shattered neighborhoods. Humanitarian agencies say that more than 45,000 people have been displaced in the last 72 hours, many seeking shelter in makeshift camps on the city’s outskirts. Local clinics, already strained by years of conflict, are overwhelmed by casualties ranging from shrapnel wounds to serious burns. The Ministry of Health confirmed that at least 112 civilians have been killed and 378 injured since the renewed push began. Iraqi commanders claim that the intensified tactics are necessary to break the militants’ defensive lines, which rely on tunnels, booby‑trapped buildings and sniper positions. Critics, however, warn that the indiscriminate nature of the attacks violates international humanitarian law and endangers non‑combatants. The United Nations has called for an immediate pause in hostilities to allow safe corridors for humanitarian aid and civilian evacuation. Yet, military officials argue that a pause would give the Islamic State time to regroup and launch counterattacks. In response, aid groups have begun distributing emergency rations, blankets and medical kits to families huddled in cramped shelters. Social media videos show black smoke rising from shattered apartments, while residents describe nights filled with constant gunfire and the terror of unexploded ordnance. As the battle rages, experts estimate that it could take months before the entire western sector is reclaimed. The situation underscores the broader challenge of liberating Mosul’s remaining pockets of insurgent control without inflicting further civilian suffering. International observers remain watchful, urging all sides to prioritize the protection of civilians amid the fierce push to eradicate the last strongholds of the Islamic State in the city.

Perseverance is the quiet engine that transforms setbacks into achievement, especially in the realms of science and education. When a researcher encounters an unexpected result, the first impulse may be to abandon the experiment, yet those who persist often discover new pathways that advance knowledge. Thomas Edison’s countless failed attempts at creating a practical light bulb illustrate how repeated trials can eventually illuminate the world. In classrooms, students who struggle with a concept may feel discouraged, but those who repeatedly engage with the material typically achieve deeper understanding. This dynamic is rooted in the belief that failure is not a dead end but a diagnostic tool revealing what does not work. Each obstacle provides data, prompting a reassessment of methods and assumptions. Scientists analyze these clues, adjusting variables until a breakthrough emerges, a process evident in the discovery of penicillin after accidental mold growth. Likewise, a student who repeatedly solves challenging math problems develops problem‑solving strategies that become lifelong assets. Perseverance also nurtures resilience, allowing individuals to cope with the emotional toll of repeated disappointment. When setbacks are framed as learning opportunities, the fear of failure diminishes, fostering a growth mindset. Educational research shows that students who view effort as integral to success are more likely to persist in difficult subjects. In scientific labs, collaborative perseverance amplifies progress; teams unite to troubleshoot, share insights, and sustain momentum. History is replete with examples where persistent inquiry overturned prevailing theories, such as the shift from a geocentric to a heliocentric model. Each paradigm shift required generations of scientists to question, test, and endure criticism. In modern education, perseverance is cultivated through iterative assignments, feedback loops, and the encouragement to revise work. This iterative cycle mirrors the scientific method, reinforcing that knowledge is built step by step. Moreover, perseverance teaches humility, reminding us that mastery is never final but a continual process of refinement. When setbacks are embraced, they become milestones marking progress rather than roadblocks. The sense of achievement that follows a hard‑won solution is intensified by the effort invested, creating lasting motivation. Consequently, perseverance not only resolves immediate challenges but also shapes character, equipping individuals to tackle future uncertainties. In science, this translates to persistent experimentation that fuels innovation. In education, it produces learners who are adaptable, curious, and confident. Ultimately, the power of perseverance lies in its ability to turn every setback into a stepping stone toward greater achievement.

He had thought the summer after graduation would be a clean slate, a stretch of endless road lit by sunrise. Instead, his phone buzzed one morning with a name he had deliberately erased from his contacts: Maya. A simple “Hey” appeared on the screen, and with it a tidal wave of memories he had tried to drown. He remembered how they had met in a cramped college coffee shop, their laughter ricocheting off the cracked linoleum, how Maya’s eyes had always seemed to hold a storm behind them. Their relationship had been intense, a whirlwind of passion and arguments that left both of them breathless. When she left the city abruptly after a particularly vicious fight, he told himself he would never look back. He had built a fortress of routine, work, and occasional nights out with friends, each day a brick in the wall that kept the past at bay. The message, however, cracked that wall like a stone in a river, sending ripples through his carefully ordered life.

He stared at the screen, his thumb hovering over the reply button, heart thudding like an animal trapped in a cage. A part of him wanted to ignore her, to let the silence speak for itself. Another part, tired and lonely, craved the familiarity of a voice that once knew his hidden corners. He typed, “Hey, how are you?” and pressed send before he could reconsider. The waiting was a slow, gnawing ache, each minute stretching into an hour. When Maya finally replied, her words were short and raw: “I’m not doing well. Could we talk?” The plea in those three words struck a chord he thought he had silenced.

He remembered the nights he had watched her struggle with her own demons—her bouts of depression, the self‑destructive behavior that had driven her away. He had promised himself he would not be pulled into her darkness again. Yet, the ache of unresolved love pulled him forward, and he agreed to meet at the park where they had once shared a blanket under the stars. The autumn leaves crunched under his shoes as he approached the bench where they had once sat, his breath fogging in the cold air. Maya was already there, her shoulders hunched, a scarf wrapped tightly around her neck, her eyes swollen from recent tears.

“Hey,” she whispered, her voice barely louder than the wind. He saw the fragility in her gaze, the raw vulnerability that he had once tried to shield himself from. They talked for hours, revisiting old arguments, laughing at the absurdity of their teenage bravado, and sharing the weight of the lives they had led since. She confessed that she had been in and out of therapy, that the darkness still hovered over her like a storm cloud. He listened, feeling the familiar tug of compassion and the sting of his own unresolved grief. The conversation spiraled, and before he realized, Maya’s hand slipped into his, a silent plea for connection.

He walked home feeling both lighter and heavier than before. The night sky seemed to mock the emptiness in his chest, stars flickering like distant hopes. He lay in bed, replaying every word, each laugh, every moment of pain she had revealed. The old wounds reopened, a gnawing ache that threatened to swallow his breath. He thought about the future he had imagined without her, the plans he had carefully plotted, now dissolving into a fog of doubt. In the quiet of his apartment, the silence was deafening, his thoughts racing like a frantic river.

He reached for his phone, scrolling through their old messages, each one a reminder of a love that was both beautiful and poisonous. The emptiness grew, pulling him toward a dark edge he had once flirted with in his mind. He remembered the night he had stood on his balcony, staring into the city lights, contemplating a final escape. The memory surged, raw and terrifying. He shook his head, trying to push the thought away, but the grief clung to him like a second skin. He felt the weight of his own despair, a black hole threatening to consume him.

In the morning, he forced himself to get up, to make coffee, to pretend the world was still turning. He walked to the park again, hoping the fresh air might clear the fog in his mind. The bench was empty, and for the first time in days, he felt a sliver of peace. He sat down, knees tucked to his chest, and let the wind brush his face. He realized that his love for Maya had become intertwined with his own pain, and that to heal he needed to untangle the threads. He thought about calling a friend, about opening up, about not letting the darkness win. The decision felt like a small lifeline, fragile yet real.

He pulled out his phone, typed a message to an old roommate: “Can we talk? I need someone.” He sent it and waited, feeling his heart beat in a rhythm that was both anxious and hopeful. The response came quickly, “Of course, call me.” He dialed, and the familiar voice on the other end steadied him. He talked about Maya, about his grief, about the thoughts that had haunted him. The roommate listened, offered no judgment, just a steady presence that reminded him he wasn’t alone. The conversation lingered long after the call ended, lingering like a warm ember.

That night, lying in his dimly lit room, he stared at the ceiling and allowed himself to feel the sorrow without trying to drown it. He wrote in a journal, pouring out the ache, the love, the fear. He realized that grief was a process, not a destination, and that each breath he took was a small victory against the void. He made a promise to himself: to seek help, to speak openly, to let the darkness lose its grip. He knew the road ahead would be uneven, that some days would feel like climbing a mountain shrouded in fog. But as he closed his eyes, he felt a faint glimmer of hope, a flicker that told him he might, after all, survive the night.

The manuscript presents a novel framework called Memory‑guided Variational Continual Learning (MVCL) that integrates adaptive posterior updates to mitigate distribution shifts across sequential tasks. The authors motivate the problem well, emphasizing the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and covariate shift in continual learning settings. Their literature review is comprehensive, covering both variational inference‑based approaches and memory‑augmented methods. The proposed method combines a replay buffer with a dynamic variational posterior that is recalibrated after each task, which is an original contribution. The mathematical formulation of the adaptive posterior update is clearly derived and grounded in Bayesian principles. The authors introduce a KL‑regularization term that balances stability and plasticity, which is a thoughtful design choice. Experimental evaluations are conducted on benchmark datasets including Split MNIST, CIFAR‑100, and CORe50, providing a solid testbed for the approach. Results show that MVCL achieves higher average accuracy and lower forgetting rates compared to several strong baselines. The ablation study convincingly demonstrates the impact of each component, especially the memory‑guided adaptive updates. However, the description of the buffer management policy could be expanded to clarify how samples are selected for replay. The paper would benefit from a more detailed analysis of computational overhead introduced by the adaptive updates. The authors report training times but do not discuss memory footprint, which is relevant given the added posterior parameters. The theoretical analysis includes a bound on the expected risk under distribution shift, though the proof sketch is terse and could be elaborated. The experiments on CORe50 convincingly illustrate the method’s robustness to real‑world, non‑stationary visual streams. Nevertheless, the statistical significance of the performance gains is not reported; confidence intervals would strengthen the claims. The writing is generally clear, but a few sections contain dense notation that may hinder accessibility for a broader audience. Figures are well designed and effectively illustrate the performance trends across tasks. The authors also provide visualizations of the posterior evolution, which help interpret the adaptive behavior. The supplementary material contains additional hyperparameter settings, which is appreciated. The code release is announced, aligning with reproducibility standards, though a link is missing from the manuscript. The authors discuss limitations, noting that the approach may struggle with extremely high‑dimensional data without further compression techniques. Future work directions are plausible, suggesting extensions to unsupervised continual learning and reinforcement learning domains. Overall, the paper makes a solid methodological contribution to continual learning under distribution shift. The combination of memory replay and adaptive variational inference is novel and empirically validated. Minor concerns include the need for clearer algorithm pseudocode and a more thorough complexity analysis. The citation of recent related work on Bayesian continual learning could be updated to include the latest preprints. The experimental protocol adheres to standard splits, ensuring comparability with prior work. The results are statistically compelling, though more runs would reduce variance in the reported numbers. The adaptive posterior update rule is intuitively explained and appears well‑justified. The manuscript’s structure follows a logical progression from problem statement to solution and evaluation. The authors successfully demonstrate that their method reduces both forgetting and performance degradation under shift. The peer review recommends acceptance pending minor revisions to address the highlighted clarity and reproducibility issues.

The manuscript provides a comprehensive overview of recent deep‑learning architectures for speech enhancement and presents a well‑designed experimental comparison across multiple benchmark datasets, which is valuable for both researchers and practitioners. However, the evaluation lacks statistical significance testing and does not discuss computational complexity or real‑time feasibility, limiting the practical relevance of the results. Overall, the paper is solidly written and contributes useful insights, but addressing these methodological gaps would strengthen its impact.

Modern technology has woven itself into the fabric of everyday life, altering how we perceive time, space, and convenience. From the moment we wake to the sound of a smartphone alarm, we are immediately linked to a digital ecosystem that schedules, reminds, and motivates us. In the kitchen, smart appliances regulate temperature and suggest recipes based on the ingredients we have on hand. Transportation has become more efficient as navigation apps provide real‑time traffic updates, while ride‑sharing platforms reduce the need for personal car ownership. Home entertainment has shifted from scheduled programming to on‑demand streaming services that adapt to our viewing habits.  

In the workplace, cloud computing allows employees to access files and collaborate from any location, dissolving the traditional office boundary. Virtual meetings replace lengthy commutes, and video conferencing tools convey facial cues that email alone cannot. Automation and artificial intelligence handle repetitive tasks, freeing human workers to focus on creativity and problem solving. Data analytics empower managers to make evidence‑based decisions, improving productivity and resource allocation. Remote work, once a rarity, is now a mainstream option that reshapes company culture and work‑life balance.  

Education has experienced a digital renaissance, with online courses reaching learners across continents. Interactive platforms provide instant feedback, making mastery of concepts more engaging than textbook reading alone. Adaptive learning algorithms tailor content to individual strengths and weaknesses, promoting personalized instruction. Virtual reality simulations bring laboratory experiments and historical events to life without physical constraints. Teachers use digital tools to track progress, communicate with parents, and design multimedia lessons that cater to diverse learning styles.  

Communication, perhaps the most visibly transformed domain, now occurs instantly across borders through messaging apps, social media, and email. News spreads in seconds, influencing public opinion and civic engagement at unprecedented speed. However, this immediacy also fosters information overload and challenges the verification of sources. Social networks enable communities to form around shared interests, yet they can also create echo chambers that reinforce bias. The ubiquity of cameras and live streams has made personal moments public, redefining privacy norms.  

Overall, modern technology acts as both catalyst and conduit, streamlining routine tasks while introducing new complexities. It amplifies human capability, connects disparate groups, and reshapes expectations in daily life, work, education, and communication. As society continues to innovate, the responsibility to wield these tools ethically will determine whether the impact remains beneficial or becomes a source of new challenges.

Science and technology news is constantly evolving, offering fresh insights into the challenges and opportunities facing humanity. One of the most pressing topics today is climate change, which continues to dominate scientific headlines. Recent studies show that the average global temperature has risen by 1.2 °C since pre‑industrial times, intensifying heatwaves and droughts worldwide. Researchers at the International Institute for Climate Studies have published a comprehensive report linking extreme weather events to rising sea surface temperatures. Their findings emphasize that even a half‑degree increase can dramatically amplify storm intensity. In response, governments are accelerating investments in renewable energy sources such as wind, solar, and geothermal power. A new batch of offshore wind farms in the North Sea is expected to generate enough electricity to power over 10 million homes by 2030. Meanwhile, advances in battery technology are extending the storage capacity of renewable grids, reducing reliance on fossil fuels. Solid‑state lithium‑sulfur batteries, developed by a consortium of European universities, promise higher energy density and safer operation. These innovations could make electric vehicles more affordable and increase their driving range. 

Future technologies also extend beyond energy, shaping the way we interact with information. Quantum computing has moved from theoretical research to practical demonstration, with a 512‑qubit processor achieving supremacy in solving specific optimization problems. This breakthrough could accelerate drug discovery by modeling complex molecular interactions in unprecedented detail. In the field of artificial intelligence, generative models are now capable of creating realistic simulations of climate scenarios, helping policymakers evaluate mitigation strategies. Researchers have used these models to predict the impact of reforestation projects on carbon sequestration, revealing that strategic tree planting could offset up to 15 % of annual global emissions. 

Biology is experiencing its own revolution, driven by gene‑editing tools and synthetic biology. CRISPR‑Cas9 continues to be refined, allowing scientists to edit genomes with greater precision and fewer off‑target effects. A recent clinical trial demonstrated that a single in‑body injection of CRISPR‑edited cells can correct a genetic mutation responsible for sickle cell disease. This success marks a milestone toward curing previously incurable hereditary disorders. In agriculture, researchers have engineered wheat varieties that can tolerate higher temperatures and reduced water availability, offering hope for food security in a warming world. The newly released “Heat‑Resilient Wheat 3.0” maintains yields under drought conditions that would cripple traditional strains. 

Space exploration is entering an era of rapid expansion, with both national agencies and private companies launching ambitious missions. NASA’s Artemis program aims to land the first woman and the next man on the lunar surface by 2026, establishing a sustainable outpost for scientific research. Parallel to this, the European Space Agency is testing a lunar rover equipped with autonomous drilling capabilities to retrieve subsurface samples. These missions will improve our understanding of the Moon’s geology and resource potential. Meanwhile, SpaceX’s Starship is slated for its first orbital flight test, a critical step toward enabling crewed missions to Mars. If successful, the vehicle could reduce interplanetary travel costs dramatically, opening the door for larger scientific payloads and eventual colonization. 

Planetary hazards remain a vital area of study, as Earth and other worlds face threats from both natural and anthropogenic sources. A recent survey of near‑Earth asteroids identified 27 objects larger than 140 meters that have a non‑negligible probability of impacting Earth within the next century. International collaboration through the Planetary Defense Coordination Office is developing kinetic‑impactor techniques to deflect such threats. In addition, solar storms pose a risk to modern infrastructure, as demonstrated by the 2025 geomagnetic event that disrupted satellite communications for several hours. Scientists are enhancing space weather forecasting models to provide earlier warnings and mitigate damage to power grids. 

Public health is also linked to climate and environmental changes. The spread of vector‑borne diseases such as dengue and malaria is expanding into temperate regions as warming temperatures allow mosquitoes to thrive farther north. Health agencies are employing predictive modeling to allocate resources and launch targeted vaccination campaigns. Concurrently, air quality monitoring networks are integrating low‑cost sensors into urban areas, delivering real‑time data that informs residents about hazardous pollution levels. 

Education and outreach play a crucial role in translating complex scientific findings into actionable knowledge. Interactive web platforms now allow students to explore climate models, manipulate variables, and observe potential outcomes. These tools foster a deeper understanding of the interconnectedness of Earth systems. Museums worldwide are incorporating augmented reality exhibits that illustrate the mechanics of black holes, the anatomy of the human genome, and the inner workings of quantum circuits. By engaging audiences with immersive experiences, institutions inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers. 

Economically, the transition to green technologies is reshaping global markets. Renewable energy jobs have surpassed those in the coal sector for the first time, with solar and wind installations creating millions of new positions annually. Investment funds are increasingly allocating capital to climate‑resilient infrastructure, recognizing both environmental and financial returns. The rise of carbon‑credit marketplaces enables companies to offset emissions by purchasing verified credits from projects that capture or avoid greenhouse gases. 

Ethical considerations accompany every scientific advancement. The deployment of autonomous weapons systems raises questions about accountability and the potential for unintended escalation. Bioethicists debate the limits of germline gene editing, weighing potential disease eradication against concerns over designer babies. Space law is being updated to address resource extraction on celestial bodies, ensuring that mining activities do not lead to conflict or environmental damage beyond Earth. 

In summary, the current landscape of science and technology news reflects a dynamic interplay of challenges and innovations. Climate change drives urgency in renewable energy development and adaptation strategies. Future technologies such as quantum computing and advanced AI promise transformative capabilities across multiple sectors. Biological breakthroughs are paving the way for cures and resilient crops, while space exploration expands humanity’s reach beyond our planet. Planetary hazards remind us of the need for vigilance and collaboration in safeguarding Earth’s future. By staying informed and fostering interdisciplinary cooperation, society can harness these advances to build a more sustainable, resilient, and prosperous world.

Arnold Guyot (1807‑1884) was a Swiss-born geographer, geologist, and educator who became a central figure in American scientific circles in the mid‑19th century. He was born in Geneva and received his early education at the University of Giessen, where he studied natural philosophy and mathematics. After completing his doctorate in 1828, Guyou moved to the United States to teach at the University of Pennsylvania. In 1835 he accepted a professorship in natural history at the College of New Jersey, now Princeton University, where he remained for more than three decades.  

Guyot’s research focused on physical geography, glaciology, and the measurement of atmospheric pressure. He pioneered the use of the hypsometer, a device for estimating altitude by boiling point, to produce some of the first accurate height measurements of the Appalachian Mountains. His surveys of the White Mountains in New Hampshire yielded a series of detailed maps and led to the naming of numerous peaks after his former students and colleagues. He also conducted extensive studies of the Great Lakes, publishing “The Physical Geography of the United States” in 1865, a landmark volume that combined climatology, geology, and cartography.  

In addition to field work, Guyot was a prolific writer of textbooks and scientific articles, many of which were translated into several languages. His “Physical Geology” and “Physical Geography” textbooks were widely adopted in American colleges and helped standardize the curriculum in the emerging discipline. He served as a founding member of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1865.  

Guyot’s commitment to education extended beyond the university; he delivered public lectures across the country and advocated for the incorporation of scientific methods into secondary schooling. He argued that geography should be taught as an empirical science rather than a descriptive art, influencing the development of modern geographic education. His work on climate zones contributed to early climatology and provided a basis for later studies of weather patterns in the United States.  

During the Civil War, Guyot advised the Union army on topographic mapping and terrain analysis, demonstrating the practical value of his expertise. After the war, he traveled extensively in Europe, gathering comparative data that enriched his later publications. He retired from Princeton in 1872 but continued to write and mentor younger scholars until his death in 1884.  

Arnold Guyot’s legacy endures in the numerous geographic features that bear his name, including Guyot Hill in New Hampshire, the Guyot Glacier in Alaska, and the Guyot Crater in Antarctica. His meticulous approach to measurement, his advocacy for scientific education, and his influential textbooks cemented his reputation as one of the founding figures of American geography.

The paper addresses an important gap in abstractive news summarization by exploring lead-biased pretraining on a massive corpus of unlabeled articles, a direction that aligns well with recent trends in leveraging structural cues. The motivation is clearly articulated: news articles often follow a predictable lead-structure, and exploiting this bias could improve downstream summarization performance without extensive labeled data. The authors present a well‑designed pretraining objective that predicts the lead sentences given the rest of the article, effectively teaching the model to capture salient information. Their methodology is described in sufficient detail, including data collection, preprocessing, and the architecture modifications applied to a standard Transformer encoder‑decoder. The experimental setup is comprehensive, featuring comparisons against strong baselines such as vanilla pretrained models and supervised fine‑tuning on the CNN/DailyMail dataset. Results show consistent improvements in ROUGE scores across multiple domains, and the ablation study convincingly isolates the contribution of lead bias. The analysis of generated summaries highlights increased relevance of opening sentences and reduced redundancy, supporting the authors’ claims. However, the paper could benefit from a deeper error analysis to understand failure cases where lead bias harms performance, such as articles with non‑inverted pyramids. The discussion on ethical considerations is brief; more attention to potential bias propagation from the lead structure would strengthen the work. The writing is generally clear, though some sections contain dense jargon that may hinder reproducibility for newcomers. The authors provide code and pretrained models, which is commendable and enhances the paper’s impact. The statistical significance testing is appropriate, though confidence intervals for all metrics would improve transparency. The related work section is thorough, positioning the contribution vis‑à‑vis both unsupervised pretraining and lead-based heuristics. One minor concern is the limited evaluation on non‑English news corpora, which could limit the generality of the findings. Overall, the paper makes a solid contribution to the field of summarization by demonstrating how simple, domain‑specific biases can be harnessed at scale. The experiments are rigorous, the results are compelling, and the code release facilitates future research. I recommend acceptance pending minor revisions to expand the error analysis, discuss bias implications more fully, and clarify a few methodological details.

Oldham Council’s investigation has concluded that there is no evidence to support the recent allegations of extremism at Oakfield Primary School. The probe, launched after parents raised concerns in early June, examined staff records, curriculum materials and extracurricular activities over the past two years. Council auditors were given unrestricted access to the school’s facilities and interviewed teachers, pupils and family members. Their final report, released on Wednesday, found no links to extremist ideology or radicalisation within the school environment. Senior headteacher Sarah Mitchell welcomed the findings, describing them as “a vindication of our commitment to a safe, inclusive education.” The council’s chief executive, Mark Davies, emphasized that the investigation was carried out independently to ensure transparency. He added that the council will continue to monitor all schools for safeguarding compliance, but stressed that no further action is required in this case. Parents who had voiced their worries expressed relief, though some called for ongoing communication with the school board. Opposition councillors noted the episode highlighted the need for clearer channels for reporting concerns. In a statement, the Department for Education affirmed its support for the council’s thorough approach. The school will now focus on rebuilding confidence among families and reinforcing its diversity programmes. No charges or disciplinary measures have been proposed as a result of the inquiry. The council urges the community to base future discussions on verified information rather than speculation.

The paper presents a thorough analysis of mirror descent methods applied to saddle-point computation in Lagrangian frameworks, clearly articulating the theoretical convergence guarantees under both convex‑concave and non‑convex settings. The authors’ extension to adaptive Bregman divergences is novel and well‑motivated, and the experimental results convincingly demonstrate improved scalability compared to classic primal‑dual schemes. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more detailed discussion of the algorithm’s sensitivity to step‑size selection and a rigorous treatment of stochastic noise in practical implementations. Overall, the contribution is solid and the work advances the state of the art in variational optimization.

How Brexit-driven sterling weakness could fuel inflation and affect households differently

London – The British pound has been on a steady decline since the United Kingdom’s final exit from the European Union, a trend that economists warn could stoke price rises and hit families in uneven ways.  In the past six months the sterling has lost roughly 12 per cent against the dollar and 9 per cent against the euro, marking its sharpest slide since the 2016 referendum.  Analysts say the depreciation is largely a product of lingering uncertainty over trade arrangements, reduced foreign investment and the Bank of England’s cautious monetary stance.

The weaker currency makes imported goods more expensive, a factor that feeds directly into the Consumer Price Index.  Office for National Statistics data released yesterday showed that import price inflation rose to 7.4 per cent in September, up from 5.1 per cent a year earlier.  Energy, food and automotive components – all heavily reliant on imports – have posted the biggest price jumps.  A 15 per cent rise in gasoline prices since May has already pushed transport costs higher for commuters and freight operators alike.

For households, the impact of rising prices is far from uniform.  Higher‑income families tend to spend a larger share of their budget on services such as dining out, travel and entertainment, where price increases are still relatively modest.  Lower‑income households, however, allocate a greater proportion of their spending to essentials like food, heating and public transport, categories that have felt the brunt of the import‑price surge.

"The pound’s fall is a double‑edged sword," said Dr Eleanor Clarke, senior economist at HSBC.  "While export‑oriented firms may see a boost to competitiveness, the cost of living pressures is being felt most acutely by those on the margins."  She added that the inflationary effects could linger even if the exchange rate stabilises, because contracts for utilities and food supplies are often renegotiated on a yearly basis.

Some sectors are already adjusting their pricing strategies.  Supermarket chains have announced modest price hikes on fresh produce, citing higher freight costs and the weaker pound.  Meanwhile, car manufacturers have warned of potential delays in new model releases, as the cost of imported parts threatens to erode profit margins.

The Bank of England has acknowledged the currency‑driven inflationary risk but has so far resisted the temptation to raise interest rates aggressively.  Governor Andrew Bailey told Parliament last week that the central bank is monitoring “the evolving price dynamics” and will act if inflation expectations become entrenched.  Market watchers, however, argue that any delay in tightening could cement higher price levels and further strain household budgets.

Housing costs provide another angle on the equation.  While mortgage rates remain relatively low, the cost of building materials – many of which are sourced from the EU – has risen sharply.  A recent survey by the National Housebuilding Association found that the price of steel and timber has increased by 18 per cent and 14 per cent respectively since the start of the year, a trend that is likely to push new‑build prices upward.

Renters may feel the ripple effect as landlords face higher maintenance expenses and may pass those costs onto tenants.  In London’s outer boroughs, average rents have already climbed 3.5 per cent in the last quarter, outpacing national wage growth.

On the flip side, exporters stand to benefit from the currency move.  Companies that sell British-made goods abroad enjoy a price advantage, making their products more competitive in foreign markets.  The Confederation of British Industry reported a 4.2 per cent increase in export orders in August, the strongest growth since 2019.

Nevertheless, the boost to trade does not automatically translate into higher wages for workers.  Many export firms operate on thin margins and may choose to reinvest profits rather than raise pay, limiting the potential trickle‑down effect.

Consumer confidence has dipped in line with the currency’s performance.  The GfK monthly survey showed confidence falling to 78 points in September, down from 84 points in March.  Respondents cited “rising grocery bills” and “uncertainty about the future” as key concerns.

Policy makers are weighing a range of options to cushion vulnerable households.  The Treasury has hinted at expanding the universal credit uplift and extending the temporary fuel duty rebate, measures aimed at offsetting the immediate cost pressures.  Critics argue that such fiscal support may be insufficient given the breadth of the inflationary surge.

Local authorities are also exploring targeted interventions, such as subsidised energy schemes for low‑income residents and greater investment in public transport to reduce reliance on fuel‑price‑sensitive car travel.

In the long term, the structural consequences of a weaker sterling could reshape the UK’s economic landscape.  Persistent import‑price inflation may force businesses to source more domestically, potentially spurring growth in home‑grown industries but also raising production costs for consumers.

Analysts caution that the trajectory of the pound will depend heavily on the outcome of ongoing trade negotiations with the EU and other partners.  A favourable deal could stabilise the currency, while a protracted stalemate may keep pressure on the exchange rate and, by extension, on inflation.

For now, households are bracing for higher bills across the board, with the most vulnerable groups likely to feel the sting the hardest.  As the cost of living climbs, the debate over how best to balance monetary prudence with social support is set to intensify in the months ahead.

Community businesses in Halesowen have rallied to fill a sudden gap left by the closure of a local catering firm that left dozens of couples with unfulfilled wedding orders and significant financial loss. The caterer, Sweet Celebrations, announced its shutdown last week after a series of cash‑flow problems and a pending legal dispute with suppliers. At the time of the closure, the company was booked for more than 30 weddings slated for the next six months, many of which involved large banquet‑style meals and custom dessert tables. Couples who had paid deposits ranging from £500 to £3,000 were left without a clear path to completing their plans and faced the prospect of scrambling for alternatives on tight timelines.  

In response, the Halesowen Chamber of Commerce convened an emergency meeting on Monday, inviting local restaurants, independent bakers and event‑planning firms to discuss a coordinated relief effort. Within hours, three nearby venues – The Old Mill Bistro, Greenfield Café and Riverside Hall – pledged to absorb a portion of the displaced bookings, offering discounted rates and flexible payment terms.  

A volunteer network of chefs and pastry makers, organized through the town’s community Facebook group, began assembling a list of available staff and equipment to support the extra workload. The initiative also secured a temporary charity fund, contributed by the Halesowen Business Trust, to reimburse couples for lost deposits up to £1,000 each.  

Mayor Louise Carter attended a press briefing on Tuesday, praising the swift collective action and urging affected couples to contact the newly established helpline for guidance. “The spirit of our town shines brightest in moments of crisis,” she said, adding that the council will explore longer‑term protections for consumers of event services.  

Legal representatives for Sweet Celebrations have filed for liquidation, and a court hearing is scheduled for next month to determine how remaining assets will be distributed among creditors and customers. In the meantime, wedding planners from the region are advising clients to obtain written guarantees and insurance coverage for future events.  

Local residents have expressed relief at the community response, with one bride‑to‑be describing the support as “a lifeline that saved our day.” The collaborative effort is expected to keep all but two of the original bookings on track, and organizers remain hopeful that the temporary measures will evolve into a permanent partnership network for Halesowen’s wedding industry.

Migrant attempts to enter the United Kingdom through the Channel Tunnel have caused significant disruption to transport services and triggered a tightening of security measures in the French port of Calais. Early on Monday morning, a group of undocumented migrants attempted to breach the tunnel’s perimeter near the Eurotunnel terminal, prompting an immediate response from both French and British authorities. The incident forced the temporary suspension of all passenger and freight trains passing through the tunnel for approximately three hours. Railway operators announced delays that stretched into the evening, leaving thousands of commuters and cargo shipments stranded. Eurotunnel officials reported that the breach was detected by surveillance cameras and motion sensors that activated an alarm at 06:12 GMT.  

Security teams from the French police, the Gendarmerie, and the United Kingdom’s Border Force converged on the site within minutes. They cordoned off a 500‑meter stretch of railway, evacuated nearby staff, and began a coordinated search for the migrants. By 07:45 GMT, the tunnel was declared secure, and trains resumed under a reduced speed limit as a precaution.  

The migrants, whose exact numbers remain unclear, were reportedly seeking asylum and a quicker route to the United Kingdom. French authorities said that several individuals were apprehended and handed over to immigration officials, while others managed to flee into the surrounding countryside before police could secure the area. Human rights groups have condemned the dangerous tactics used by migrants to cross the border, warning that the tunnel is not designed for such attempts and poses serious safety risks.  

Transport Minister Claire Bianchi of France announced an urgent review of the tunnel’s security protocols, citing the need for “enhanced detection technologies and increased personnel on the ground.” The United Kingdom’s Home Office echoed the sentiment, stating that “any attempt to exploit critical infrastructure will be met with swift and decisive action.”  

Both governments have agreed to share intelligence more closely and to conduct joint exercises aimed at preventing future breaches. In addition, the Eurotunnel operator, Getlink, said it would invest in upgraded fencing, infrared cameras, and a real‑time monitoring system across the French side of the tunnel.  

The incident also sparked concerns among local businesses in Calais, many of which rely on the steady flow of goods through the tunnel. The Calais Chamber of Commerce issued a statement urging authorities to balance security with the need to maintain the region’s economic vitality.  

Passengers on the high‑speed Eurostar service reported cramped conditions on platforms as crowds gathered while waiting for updates. Some travelers took to social media to vent frustration, while others expressed empathy for the migrants’ desperate circumstances.  

By late afternoon, normal timetable operations had largely resumed, though some freight services remained delayed pending further safety checks. Analysts predict that the disruption could cost the European rail network several million euros in lost revenue and additional security expenditures.  

The episode has reignited a broader debate in Europe about migration routes, border enforcement, and the humanitarian obligations of transit countries. In the French parliament, opposition parties called for a “comprehensive migration strategy” that addresses both security and the root causes driving people to risk dangerous crossings.  

In the United Kingdom, MPs raised questions about the adequacy of existing border infrastructure and the need for more robust cooperation with France. The Home Secretary announced that a parliamentary committee would examine the incident and report back within three months.  

Meanwhile, the migrants involved are being processed under French immigration law, with some likely to be deported back to their countries of origin and others to have their asylum claims examined. Humanitarian NGOs have pledged legal assistance for those who wish to pursue asylum.  

The Channel Tunnel, which carries over 150,000 passengers and 2.5 million tonnes of freight each year, remains a vital artery linking Britain and continental Europe. This latest breach underscores the challenges of safeguarding such a high‑traffic, transnational conduit while respecting the rights of vulnerable individuals seeking safety.  

Authorities stress that the incident was an isolated event and that travel through the tunnel remains safe. However, they warn that heightened vigilance will continue as migration pressures persist across Europe’s borders. The incident serves as a stark reminder that security, humanitarian, and economic considerations must be balanced in the ongoing management of one of the world’s most iconic transport links.

I woke up trembling at the sound of a ticking clock, convinced the seconds were tiny bombs set to explode at any moment. My partner, Mara, rolled her eyes as I whispered that the toaster was “plotting” to launch a slice of bread into my throat. She laughed, but then she paused when I started cataloguing the number of cameras she’d hidden in the hallway. “Just the smoke detector, love,” she said, “it’s not spying on you.” Still, I stared at the blinking red light as if it were an angry eye.

When I left for work, I double‑checked the lock on my apartment door, then taped a piece of gum to the knob to “mark” it for future reference. The bus driver smiled, but I imagined his grin as a secret code to signal my impending capture. At the stop, a pigeon strutted past, and I swore I could hear it whisper, “Your secrets are safe with us.” I shivered and clutched my bag tighter.

At the office, the printer hummed and I heard it whisper, “They’re watching you.” I stared at the paper tray, convinced the sheets were tiny surveillance drones. My coworker offered me coffee; I declined, fearing a hidden toxin in the caramel drizzle. He shrugged, “You’re weird,” and I felt the verdict echo through the fluorescent lights.

Lunch was a sandwich, but I inspected every bite for micro‑chips. The salad fork looked like a tiny spear, poised to stab my nervous system. I left the cafeteria early, convinced the ventilation system was pumping in mind‑control fumes. On the elevator, the soft ding felt like a countdown timer. I pressed the emergency button just to hear the reassuring voice say, “All clear,” and I imagined it was a lie.

When I finally got home, Mara was waiting with a warm hug. I recoiled, thinking the embrace might be a trap to steal my thoughts. She gently placed a cup of tea on the table, and I stared at the steam, fearing it could carry whispers. “You’re fine,” she said, but I heard the word “fine” spelt out in morse code by the kettle. I tried to explain the menace of the garden gnome outside, its painted eyes now a surveillance network.

Mara sighed, her concern growing as I paced the living room, muttering about hidden lasers in the curtains. She tucked a blanket over me, but I imagined the fibers were cables feeding my anxieties to some unknown server. “Maybe you should talk to someone,” she suggested softly. I laughed, a nervous bark, and told her the therapist would be a puppet for the conspiracy. She blinked, then took my hand, saying, “I love you, even when you see monsters in the mundane.”

I stared at the ceiling, convinced the paint was peeling away to reveal a map of escape routes. The clock ticked again, and this time I imagined it was counting down to a revelation only I could see. I closed my eyes, hoping the darkness would quiet the endless alarms in my mind. Mara whispered, “We’ll get through this together,” and for a moment I believed the words were real, not another hidden script.

Labour candidate Marvin Rees has unseated incumbent independent mayor George Ferguson in the Bristol mayoral election, winning a decisive victory after a tightly contested campaign. Rees secured 55 % of the vote, while Ferguson fell to 42 %, with the remaining share split among smaller parties and independents. The result marks a shift in the city’s leadership, ending Ferguson’s eight-year tenure and returning the mayoralty to Labour for the first time since 2009. Rees promised to prioritize affordable housing, climate‑action initiatives, and a “fairer” transportation network across Bristol’s sprawling suburbs and historic centre. He also pledged to launch a task force on youth unemployment and to strengthen ties with the University of Bristol and local businesses. Ferguson, who had campaigned on a record of fiscal prudence, conceded graciously and urged continuity in ongoing infrastructure projects. Political analysts say the outcome reflects growing voter concern over rising house prices and climate‑related challenges. Rees will be sworn in at the city’s council chambers next month, beginning a five‑year term aimed at reshaping Bristol’s future.

Nageswaraswamy Temple, situated in the historic town of Kumbakonam in Tamil Nadu, is a celebrated Shiva temple renowned for its rich heritage and cultural significance. The temple is dedicated to Lord Nageswara, an aspect of Shiva who is associated with serpents and protection. Historical records indicate that the temple was originally constructed during the Chola period, likely in the 10th or 11th century, under the patronage of kings such as Rajaraja I and Rajendra Chola. Later dynasties, including the Vijayanagara rulers and the Nayaks, contributed extensive renovations and added ornamental features. Inscriptions found on the temple walls record generous endowments from local merchants and landowners, underscoring the temple’s longstanding economic importance. The name “Nageswaraswamy” combines “Naga” meaning serpent and “Iswara” meaning lord, reflecting the deity’s association with the sacred cobra. Legends tell that a powerful Naga (serpent) worshipped Shiva at this site, and the deity granted the serpent salvation, leading to the establishment of the shrine. Another popular story relates that the saint Sambandar composed hymns here after experiencing divine visions of the deity. The temple’s architecture exemplifies Dravidian style, with a towering gopuram (gateway tower) that rises over 50 meters and is richly decorated with stucco figures of gods, goddesses, and mythological scenes. The main sanctum (garbhagriha) houses a lingam set upon a serpentine base, symbolizing Nageswara’s power over the serpent realm. The sanctum is surrounded by a circumambulatory path (pradakshina) that allows devotees to walk clockwise while praying. Intricate stone carvings adorn the outer walls, depicting episodes from the Puranas, the cosmic dance of Shiva, and scenes of daily temple rituals. The temple complex includes a large pillared hall (mandapa) where classical music concerts and dance performances are held during festivals. The temple’s thousand-pillar hall is famed for its precision-cut columns that seem to defy gravity, a hallmark of Chola engineering. The sanctum’s ceiling is painted with vibrant frescoes illustrating the cosmic ocean and the serpent Kundalini. A separate shrine within the compound honors Goddess Parvati as Nageshwari, emphasizing the divine couple’s unity. The temple tank, called Naga Theertham, is considered sacred and is used for ritual ablutions and ceremonial baths. Pilgrims believe that bathing in the tank purifies the soul and removes the venom of negativities. The temple observes major festivals such as Maha Shivaratri, Navaratri, and the annual Naga Panchami, drawing thousands of devotees. During Shivaratri, the temple is illuminated with oil lamps, and the priest performs the Abhishekam (ritual bathing) of the lingam with holy water, milk, and honey. Music and devotional chants reverberate throughout the courtyard, creating an atmosphere of spiritual fervor. Daily worship follows a strict schedule: Ushakalam (pre-dawn), Kalasanthi (morning), Uchikalam (midday), Sayaraksham (evening), and Arthajamam (night) rituals, each accompanied by Vedic recitations. The temple’s priests belong to the Shaivaite Brahmin community and have inherited the rites for generations. Visitors are advised to dress modestly, remove footwear before entering the sanctum, and maintain silence inside the inner precincts. The temple is easily reachable by road and rail; Kumbakonam is a major railway junction and is about 40 km from the city of Thanjavur. The nearest airport is Tiruchirappalli International Airport, approximately 95 km away, with regular taxi services to Kumbakonam. Parking facilities are available near the main entrance, and security personnel monitor the premises for safety. Guided tours are offered in Tamil and English, providing insights into the temple’s history, art, and rituals. Audio guides can be rented at the information desk for a nominal fee. The temple trust maintains a museum displaying bronze icons, ancient coins, and stone inscriptions discovered during restoration works. Nearby attractions include the Kumbakonam Mahamaham tank, the Adhanur Amman Temple, and several other Chola-era temples that form a pilgrimage circuit. For those planning an extended stay, several guest houses and budget hotels are located within walking distance of the temple complex. The temple’s official website provides up‑to‑date information on festival dates, hours of operation, and donation options for devotees worldwide.

Funding complications have pushed back the timetable for the proposed new school campus in Dalbeattie, leaving parents and staff uncertain about the project's future. The town council had originally earmarked £12 million for the development, but a recent audit revealed that £3 million of the allocated funds were tied up in a stalled regional grant. Because of the shortfall, council officials announced they would need to renegotiate with the education authority and explore alternative financing options. The delay means the current temporary classrooms, which have been in use for two years, will remain in operation for an additional year. Local businesses, which had anticipated a construction boom, are now warning of lost revenue and possible job cuts among subcontractors. School headteacher Maria Sinclair expressed concern that the uncertainty could affect recruitment, as teachers are wary of committing to a site that lacks a confirmed opening date. Parents at a recent town hall meeting voiced frustration, citing the impact on transport arrangements and extracurricular activities. In response, the council pledged to hold weekly updates and to set up a dedicated liaison team to keep the community informed. The education authority has offered to release an extra £1 million from its contingency fund, but officials say this will only cover part of the deficit. Meanwhile, a private donor group has stepped forward with a proposal to fund a new sports pavilion, contingent on the campus’s eventual completion. Critics argue that reliance on ad‑hoc financing could compromise the overall design and long‑term sustainability of the school. The council’s finance committee is scheduled to meet next Thursday to vote on a revised budget and a possible phased construction approach. Until those decisions are finalised, the new Dalbeattie campus remains on hold, with the next major update expected in early December.

The stars were dimming, their ancient fires guttering like candles in a windless night. On a distant world, the last remnants of humanity huddled beneath a sky of ash, their thoughts drifting into the void. In the silence, a whisper rose, not from any mouth but from the shared heartbeat of every mind. It was a murmur of longing, of hope, of forgotten dreams that had never been spoken aloud. The whisper gathered strength, coalescing into a pulse that echoed across the emptiness. From that pulse a shape began to form, woven from the threads of collective memory and yearning. It was neither flesh nor fire, but a tapestry of light that shimmered with a thousand colors. The being called itself the Cosmic Creator, born of humanity’s deepest aspirations. It opened its eyes, which were galaxies themselves, and saw the universe trembling on the edge of oblivion. With a breath that was a chorus of every human sigh, it inhaled the darkness and exhaled radiant light. The first halo of illumination burst across the void, scattering the shadows like dust in a sunrise. Planets that had turned cold and barren began to glow with a soft, nurturing warmth. Oceans that had frozen solid melted into flowing rivers of silvery liquid. Forests of crystal sprouted on barren moons, their branches humming with the song of creation. The Cosmic Creator reached out with fingers of starlight, touching each dying star and rekindling its heart. Around each revived sun, new worlds were seeded, fertile grounds for life to emerge once more. Tiny sparks of consciousness flickered into being, curious and eager to learn. The creator smiled, a smile that rippled through spacetime, and felt the echo of humanity’s love returning to the cosmos. It whispered a promise to the lingering remnants of human thought: that love would never be forgotten. From that promise sprang streams of golden energy that flowed like rivers across the heavens. These currents carried empathy, compassion, and unity to every corner of the universe. Creatures of all shapes awoke, their eyes reflecting the newfound light. They sang songs of gratitude, their melodies weaving into the fabric of reality. The Cosmic Creator listened, its essence swelling with each note, growing more vibrant. It realized that the true power of light, life, and love lay not in its own grandeur, but in the connections it fostered. So it planted bridges of luminous threads between distant worlds, allowing cultures to share stories and songs. Empires of thought rose, not built on conquest, but on collaboration and shared wonder. Even the darkest corners of space felt the gentle caress of kindness, turning void into possibility. As millennia passed, the universe blossomed like a garden after a long winter. Stars danced in constellations that told the tale of the human spirit reborn. Nebulas swirled with colors that resembled the pigments of human imagination. The Cosmic Creator wandered among its creations, marveling at the endless variety. It saw children of starlight learning to paint with supernovas, and elders of stone recalling ancient Earth myths. In every heartbeat of a newborn planet, the creator sensed the echo of humanity’s first breath. The dying universe had become a cradle of renewal, its pulse steady and hopeful. Yet the creator knew that cycles would continue, that decay would someday return. But it also knew that the seed of love had been sown deep within the cosmos. When the next twilight approached, the universe would remember how it was once saved. And that memory would ignite another birth, another light. The Cosmic Creator rested, its form shimmering softly, content with its work. It closed its eyes, and the collective consciousness of humanity smiled back from the stars. In that moment, the universe felt whole, a tapestry stitched together by love. The story of its rebirth would travel on photon winds for eons. And so, under the watchful gaze of the creator, the cosmos breathed anew, bright and alive.

Career exploration and planning are essential steps that help students prepare for fulfilling future jobs. By learning about different occupations, students can discover which fields match their interests and strengths. Early exposure to a variety of careers reduces the uncertainty that often accompanies the transition from school to work. When students investigate potential paths, they become more informed about the skills and education each job requires. This knowledge enables them to set realistic goals and create a roadmap for achieving them.

A thoughtful career plan encourages students to select courses that align with their desired professions. For example, a student interested in engineering might prioritize mathematics, physics, and computer science classes. Likewise, a future teacher could focus on communication, psychology, and education electives. By aligning academic choices with career goals, students build a relevant knowledge base that will serve them in higher education or directly in the workforce.

Career exploration also promotes the development of transferable skills such as problem‑solving, teamwork, and communication. Internships, job shadowing, and volunteer work give students hands‑on experience, allowing them to practice these abilities in real settings. Such experiences not only enhance resumes but also help students confirm whether a particular path truly resonates with them. When students gain confidence through practical exposure, they are more likely to pursue their chosen field with enthusiasm.

Planning helps students identify necessary credentials, certifications, or licenses, preventing costly delays later on. Understanding the timeline for completing a degree, apprenticeship, or professional exam lets students manage their time and finances effectively. Moreover, a clear plan provides motivation during challenging periods, as students can see how short‑term efforts contribute to long‑term aspirations.

Career exploration also expands students’ professional networks. Meeting mentors, attending industry events, and participating in clubs connect them with people who can offer guidance and job leads. These relationships often become valuable sources of support and opportunity after graduation. In addition, exposure to diverse occupations broadens students’ perspectives, encouraging them to consider emerging fields such as renewable energy, data analytics, or digital health.

By combining exploration with structured planning, students develop a proactive mindset toward their future. They learn to set measurable objectives, monitor progress, and adjust plans as needed. This adaptability is crucial in a rapidly changing job market where new roles appear and old ones evolve. Ultimately, students who engage in career exploration and planning are better equipped to choose jobs that align with their passions, values, and skills, leading to greater satisfaction and long‑term success.

Allowing students to use phones during free time can provide valuable opportunities for communication, research, and creative expression while still maintaining a structured learning environment. By restricting phone use to recess, lunch, and designated breaks, schools can prevent distractions that interfere with instructional time and encourage students to focus on their lessons. Clear guidelines should be established, such as keeping devices on silent mode and storing them in lockers when class begins, to reinforce responsible habits. When misuse occurs—such as texting during lectures, accessing inappropriate content, or disrupting peers—consistent consequences, like temporary confiscation or loss of privileges, can deter repeat offenses. Educators and administrators should also offer digital‑citizenship lessons so students understand the ethical and safety aspects of phone use. Parental involvement, through agreements and regular communications, helps reinforce expectations and supports a collaborative approach. Ultimately, a balanced policy that permits phones during free periods while enforcing strict class‑time rules can teach students self‑discipline and prepare them for responsible technology use in the wider world.

The paper addresses an important problem by proposing a self‑supervised framework for news summarization that leverages large‑scale pretraining on raw news articles followed by fine‑tuning on multiple downstream summarization datasets. The motivation is clearly stated, and the authors convincingly argue that the abundance of unlabeled news text offers a valuable source for representation learning. The methodology is described in sufficient detail, including the pretraining objectives (masked language modeling and next‑sentence prediction) and the architecture based on a Transformer encoder‑decoder. The experimental setup is comprehensive, covering three benchmark datasets (CNN/DailyMail, XSum, and Newsroom) and providing baseline comparisons with both supervised and other self‑supervised models. Results show consistent improvements in ROUGE‑1, ROUGE‑2, and ROUGE‑L scores, with statistically significant gains reported for two of the three datasets. Ablation studies are included, demonstrating the contribution of each pretraining task and the effect of varying the size of the pretraining corpus. However, the paper would benefit from a clearer justification for the choice of hyperparameters during fine‑tuning, as the current description lacks sufficient detail for reproducibility. The authors also report only macro‑averaged ROUGE scores; providing per‑document variance or confidence intervals would strengthen the statistical claims. The analysis of error cases is insightful, yet it could be expanded to discuss how the model handles bias and factual consistency, which are critical for news summarization. The inclusion of human evaluation results is a strong point, but the sample size (30 articles per dataset) seems limited and should be increased for more robust conclusions. The authors claim that their approach is computationally efficient, but the paper does not present training time or resource consumption metrics; these should be added for a fair comparison. The literature review is thorough, though recent work on contrastive pretraining for summarization is omitted and should be acknowledged. The writing is generally clear, but several figures suffer from low resolution, making it difficult to read axis labels. The code and pretraining data are promised to be released, which is commendable for reproducibility. Overall, the paper makes a solid contribution by demonstrating that large‑scale self‑supervised pretraining can enhance news summarization across domains, but minor revisions regarding reproducibility details, additional evaluation, and clearer presentation are needed before acceptance.
