Diagnostic accuracy of cervical screening and biopsy techniques for identifying squamous cell abnormalities in Iranian women with abnormal Pap results

Background. Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among women worldwide, with an estimated 604 000 new cases and 342 000 deaths in 2020. Persistent infection with high‑risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is the primary etiological factor for the development of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Early detection through organized screening programs has dramatically reduced incidence and mortality in high‑income countries. In Iran, cervical cancer incidence is lower than in many regions, yet the disease burden is rising due to changing sexual behaviors, increased HPV prevalence, and limited coverage of screening services. The Pap smear, introduced in the 1940s, remains the cornerstone of cervical cancer screening, but its sensitivity ranges from 50 to 75 % and specificity from 85 to 95 % when compared with histopathology. Consequently, women with abnormal cytology (ASC‑US, LSIL, HSIL, or carcinoma) are referred for colposcopic evaluation and directed biopsy. However, colposcopic impression may be subjective, and biopsy sampling errors can lead to under‑diagnosis or overtreatment. Alternative or adjunctive methods such as liquid‑based cytology (LBC), HPV DNA testing, and novel imaging modalities have been investigated to improve diagnostic accuracy. Nevertheless, the optimal combination of screening and biopsy techniques for Iranian women with abnormal Pap results remains unclear.

Objective. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of different cervical screening (conventional Pap smear, liquid‑based cytology, HPV testing) and biopsy techniques (targeted punch biopsy, random 4‑quadrant biopsy, endocervical curettage) for detecting squamous cell abnormalities in Iranian women presenting with abnormal Pap smears.

Methods. A prospective, multi‑center diagnostic accuracy study was conducted between January 2022 and December 2025 in four tertiary gynecologic oncology centers across Iran (Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz, and Mashhad). Women aged 21–65 years with a recent abnormal Pap result (ASC‑US, LSIL, HSIL, or ASC‑H) were eligible. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy, prior treatment for CIN or cervical cancer, immunosuppression, and inability to provide informed consent. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of all participating centers and adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki.

Sample size calculation assumed an expected sensitivity of 85 % for the combined screening approach, a prevalence of CIN2+ of 15 % among abnormal Pap cases, a margin of error of 5 %, and a confidence level of 95 %. The resulting required sample size was 1 200 participants; 1 254 women were enrolled to account for attrition.

Procedures. At enrollment, participants underwent a repeat conventional Pap smear and a liquid‑based cytology specimen collected using the ThinPrep® system. An aliquot of the liquid‑based sample was processed for high‑risk HPV DNA detection using the Hybrid Capture 2 assay. Results were reported according to the Bethesda 2020 system. All participants were then scheduled for colposcopic examination performed by experienced colposcopists blinded to the HPV result. Colposcopic impression was recorded using the IFCPC 2011 terminology (normal, low grade, high grade, cancer).

Biopsy protocol. For each participant, three biopsy strategies were applied sequentially: (1) targeted punch biopsy of the most abnormal area identified on colposcopy; (2) four‑quadrant random punch biopsies at the 12, 3, 6, and 9 o’clock positions irrespective of visual abnormality; and (3) endocervical curettage (ECC) performed with a curette inserted 5–10 mm into the endocervical canal. Biopsy specimens were fixed in 10 % neutral buffered formalin, embedded in paraffin, and stained with hematoxylin‑eosin. Histopathological evaluation was performed by two independent pathologists blinded to clinical data; discrepancies were resolved by consensus.

Reference standard. The composite reference standard comprised the most severe histopathological diagnosis obtained from any of the three biopsy methods or, when available, subsequent excisional procedure (LEEP or cold knife conization) performed within six weeks of colposcopy. Histologic categories were classified as negative/normal, CIN1, CIN2, CIN3, or invasive carcinoma. For analysis, CIN2+ (CIN2, CIN3, carcinoma) was considered clinically significant disease.

Statistical analysis. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and likelihood ratios were calculated for each screening test alone and in combination, using the composite reference standard as the truth. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated, and the area under the curve (AUC) compared using DeLong’s test. Pairwise comparisons of biopsy strategies employed McNemar’s test for paired proportions. Multivariate logistic regression assessed factors associated with missed CIN2+ (age, parity, HPV status, lesion size). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Analyses were performed with Stata version 18.0.

Results. Of the 1 254 enrolled women, 1 212 completed the full protocol and provided adequate specimens; 42 were excluded due to insufficient tissue or loss to follow‑up. The median age was 38 years (interquartile range 31–45). Cytology distribution at enrollment was ASC‑US (28 %), LSIL (34 %), HSIL (30 %), and ASC‑H (8 %). High‑risk HPV was detected in 68 % of participants, with HPV16 being the most common genotype (32 % of HPV‑positive cases).

Colposcopic impression classified lesions as normal (5 %), low grade (40 %), high grade (50 %), and cancer (5 %). Histopathology identified CIN2+ in 210 women (17.3 %): CIN2 (84), CIN3 (96), and invasive carcinoma (30). The remaining 1 002 women had CIN1 or negative findings.

Screening test performance. Conventional Pap smear alone yielded a sensitivity of 71 % (95 % CI 0.65–0.76) and specificity of 88 % (0.86–0.90) for CIN2+. Liquid‑based cytology improved sensitivity to 78 % (0.73–0.83) while maintaining specificity at 87 % (0.85–0.89). High‑risk HPV testing alone demonstrated a sensitivity of 92 % (0.88–0.95) but lower specificity of 61 % (0.58–0.64). Combining LBC with HPV testing increased sensitivity to 95 % (0.92–0.98) and specificity to 70 % (0.67–0.73). The AUC values were 0.79 for conventional Pap, 0.82 for LBC, 0.77 for HPV alone, and 0.85 for the combined LBC + HPV strategy (p < 0.001 for comparison).

Biopsy technique performance. Targeted punch biopsy identified CIN2+ in 180 of 210 cases, yielding a sensitivity of 86 % (0.81–0.90) and specificity of 93 % (0.91–0.95). Four‑quadrant random biopsy detected 165 cases (sensitivity 79 %, 0.73–0.84) with specificity 96 % (0.94–0.98). Endocervical curettage alone identified 120 cases (sensitivity 57 %, 0.50–0.64) but had a high specificity of 98 % (0.97–0.99). When the three methods were combined, sensitivity reached 96 % (0.92–0.99) and specificity 91 % (0.89–0.93). The incremental yield of adding random biopsies to a targeted approach was 5 % (p = 0.03), while adding ECC contributed an additional 3 % (p = 0.07, not statistically significant). The combined biopsy protocol had an AUC of 0.94, significantly higher than any single method (p < 0.001).

Predictors of missed disease. Multivariate analysis revealed that negative HPV status (adjusted odds ratio AOR 4.2, 95 % CI 2.1–8.3), lesion size < 5 mm on colposcopy (AOR 3.5, 1.9–6.4), and age > 50 years (AOR 2.1, 1.1–4.0) were independently associated with false‑negative biopsy results. Parity and smoking status were not significant predictors.

Safety and acceptability. No major complications were reported. Minor bleeding occurred in 8 % of participants and resolved spontaneously. Pain scores (0–10 visual analog scale) averaged 3.2 for targeted biopsy, 3.8 for random biopsies, and 4.1 for ECC. Patient satisfaction surveys indicated a preference for fewer biopsies when diagnostic yield was similar.

Discussion. This large prospective study demonstrates that in Iranian women with abnormal Pap results, the combination of liquid‑based cytology and high‑risk HPV testing provides the highest sensitivity for detecting CIN2+, albeit with modest specificity. Among biopsy strategies, targeted punch biopsy remains the most efficient single method, but the addition of four‑quadrant random biopsies yields a statistically significant incremental detection of high‑grade lesions, supporting a more comprehensive sampling approach in cases with equivocal colposcopic findings. Endocervical curettage contributed limited additional diagnostic value, consistent with prior literature suggesting its role is primarily for glandular lesions.

The observed sensitivity of HPV testing aligns with global data, confirming its utility as a triage tool in low‑resource settings. However, the lower specificity underscores the need for adjunctive cytology to reduce unnecessary referrals and procedures. The high prevalence of HPV16 among the study cohort mirrors patterns in other Middle Eastern populations and may inform vaccine implementation strategies.

Our findings have several implications. First, national cervical cancer screening guidelines in Iran should consider adopting a primary HPV screening algorithm with reflex LBC for HPV‑positive women, optimizing the balance between detection and resource utilization. Second, colposcopic protocols could be updated to incorporate systematic random biopsies in addition to targeted sampling, particularly when the visual impression is low grade or when lesions are small and difficult to assess. Third, training programs for colposcopists should emphasize accurate lesion mapping and adequate tissue acquisition to minimize false‑negative outcomes.

Limitations of the study include the lack of long‑term follow‑up to assess progression of missed lesions, potential verification bias since all participants underwent the reference standard, and the exclusion of women with glandular abnormalities, limiting generalizability to those populations. Additionally, the study did not evaluate emerging technologies such as optical coherence tomography or p16/Ki‑67 dual staining, which may further enhance diagnostic accuracy.

Conclusion. In Iranian women presenting with abnormal Pap smears, a combined screening approach of liquid‑based cytology and high‑risk HPV testing achieves superior sensitivity for detecting clinically significant squamous cell abnormalities. Targeted punch biopsy remains the cornerstone of histopathologic evaluation, but the routine addition of four‑quadrant random biopsies significantly improves detection of CIN2+. Endocervical curettage adds minimal value for squamous lesions. Implementation of these evidence‑based strategies could strengthen cervical cancer prevention programs in Iran, reduce the burden of missed high‑grade disease, and ultimately improve women's health outcomes.

Keywords: cervical cancer, screening, Pap smear, liquid‑based cytology, HPV DNA testing, colposcopy, targeted biopsy, random biopsy, endocervical curettage, Iran.

Ravenna, a historic city on the Adriatic coast of Italy, is celebrated for its extraordinary Byzantine mosaics. These mosaics date from the 5th to the 9th centuries, a period when Ravenna served as the capital of the Western Roman Empire and later of the Ostrogothic and Byzantine kingdoms. In 1996 UNESCO inscribed the Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna, including its mosaics, as a World Heritage Site. The designation recognizes the city’s unique contribution to the development of Christian art and architecture. Visitors to Ravenna can explore eight UNESCO‑listed monuments, each adorned with dazzling tesserae that capture light in vivid color. The Basilica of San Vitale is perhaps the most famous of these sites. Its dome features a spectacular mosaic of Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora, symbols of imperial authority and divine endorsement. The mosaic’s gold background creates a heavenly aura that still mesmerizes viewers. Adjacent to San Vitale, the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia showcases a more intimate but equally brilliant mosaic program. The ceiling of the mausoleum is covered with a star‑filled sky, a motif that has inspired countless artists. The basilica’s apse presents an image of Christ enthroned, surrounded by angels and saints, rendered in luminous blues and reds. Another UNESCO monument, the Basilica of Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, was originally built by Theodoric the Great for his Arian court. Its nave is lined with a procession of saints, each figure depicted with distinct posture and attire. The mosaics here illustrate the transition from Arian to orthodox Christianity in Ravenna. The adjacent Mausoleum of Theodoric, though not a mosaic site, adds to the city’s architectural diversity with its massive monolithic dome. Further north, the Basilica of San Apollinare in Classe, located just outside the city walls, offers a monumental mosaic of Christ the Good Shepherd. This work is lauded for its serene composition and harmonious color palette. The Lonigo Chapel, a lesser‑known gem, contains a small yet exquisite mosaic of the Virgin Mary. These mosaics collectively demonstrate the technical mastery of Byzantine artisans, who cut tiny glass and stone pieces to create intricate narratives. The use of gold leaf reflects the theological belief in light as a manifestation of the divine. Ravenna’s mosaics also reveal cultural exchanges between the Eastern Roman Empire and the Italian peninsula. Patterns borrowed from Syrian and Coptic art appear alongside Italic motifs. This synthesis contributed to the evolution of Romanesque and later Gothic styles. The city’s historical significance extends beyond its mosaics. In the 5th century, Ravenna became the seat of the Western Roman Emperor Honorius. After the fall of Rome, the Ostrogothic king Theodoric made the city his capital, preserving many of its Roman infrastructure. In 540 AD, the Byzantine general Belisarius recaptured Ravenna for Emperor Justinian, ushering in a golden age of Byzantine art. The city remained under Byzantine control until the Lombards seized it in the 8th century. Throughout these changes, Ravenna retained its status as a religious and administrative hub. The archbishopric of Ravenna was one of the most powerful in Italy, influencing ecclesiastical politics. Today, the city’s historic center is a pedestrian‑friendly area that invites leisurely exploration. The Via Garibaldi, lined with cafés and boutiques, leads visitors from the train station to the UNESCO sites. Guided tours often combine art history with anecdotes about the lives of the artists and patrons. Interactive audio guides provide translations of Latin inscriptions found in the mosaics. For families, the Museo Nazionale di Ravenna offers hands‑on workshops on mosaic making. Children can learn how to place tiny glass pieces to form simple patterns, gaining appreciation for the craft. The museum also displays archaeological finds that contextualize the mosaics within daily Roman life. Another cultural attraction is the annual Ravenna Festival, a summer event featuring opera, ballet, and classical concerts. Performances are sometimes staged inside the historic basilicas, creating an immersive acoustic experience. Culinary tourists can sample local specialties such as piadina, a thin flatbread traditionally filled with cheese and cured meats. The nearby Adriatic coast offers beaches where visitors can relax after a day of museum hopping. The city’s transport network includes a well‑connected train station that links Ravenna to Bologna, Florence, and Venice. Public buses provide easy access to the outlying archaeological sites. Bicycle rentals are popular for those who wish to explore the countryside at a slower pace. The surrounding region of Emilia‑Romagna is renowned for its gastronomic traditions, including Parmigiano‑Reggiano and balsamic vinegar. A day trip to the medieval town of Cervia allows travelers to compare different layers of Italian history. For art scholars, Ravenna serves as a case study in the preservation of fresco and mosaic techniques. Conservation teams employ non‑invasive laser cleaning to remove centuries of grime without damaging the original tesserae. Climate control systems maintain stable temperature and humidity inside the basilicas, protecting the delicate pigments. Ongoing research projects use 3‑D scanning to create digital replicas of the mosaics for virtual exhibitions. These digital tools enable scholars worldwide to study the artworks without risking physical wear. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee periodically reviews the site’s management plan to ensure sustainable tourism. Visitor limits are enforced during peak season to prevent overcrowding in the most fragile spaces. Educational programs for local schools encourage students to become stewards of their cultural heritage. Scholarships are offered to aspiring conservators who wish to specialize in Byzantine art. The city’s municipal government has partnered with private sponsors to fund restoration projects. Recent work on the dome of San Vitale restored lost gold leaf, bringing the original brilliance back to life. This restoration was documented in a short film shown at the Ravenna International Film Festival. The film highlights the collaboration between artisans, scientists, and historians. Beyond the mosaics, Ravenna boasts a lively contemporary art scene. The Palazzo d'Accursio hosts rotating exhibitions of modern artists inspired by medieval themes. Street art murals along the city walls reinterpret classic mosaic patterns in bright, abstract forms. This dialogue between old and new reflects Ravenna’s ongoing cultural vitality. Travelers seeking accommodation can choose from historic hotels housed in restored palazzos. Budget options include family‑run bed and breakfasts that serve homemade pasta. For luxury seekers, a waterfront resort offers spa treatments with ingredients sourced from local vineyards. The city’s night life centers around piazzas where locals gather for aperitivo. Live jazz bands occasionally perform near the Baptistery of Neon, adding a modern soundtrack to ancient surroundings. The Baptistery itself, dating to the 5th century, contains a remarkable mosaic of the Pentecost scene. Its octagonal dome is capped by a silver lantern that shines at sunset. The multicultural heritage of Ravenna is also evident in its religious festivals. The Feast of Saint Apollinaris, the city’s patron saint, includes processions that pass by the UNESCO sites. Participants carry candles and chant hymns that echo centuries of tradition. These events attract pilgrims from across Italy and neighboring countries. The city’s archives preserve documents written in Latin, Greek, and early Italian dialects. Scholars can request access to original charters that detail the commissioning of the mosaics. Such primary sources reveal the political motivations behind the artistic programs. For example, Emperor Justinian’s mosaics were intended to assert his authority over the western territories. The mosaics also served as visual sermons for an illiterate congregation. Their vivid storytelling made theological concepts accessible to all. In modern times, the mosaics inspire designers in fashion and interior décor. Patterns reminiscent of San Vitale appear on contemporary fabrics and wallpapers. Architects cite the harmonious proportion of Ravenna’s basilicas as models for sustainable design. The city’s blend of historical preservation and innovative use of space serves as a blueprint for other heritage sites. Visitors leave Ravenna with a deeper appreciation for how art can bridge past and present. The mosaics remind us that beauty and faith have shaped human experience for millennia. By protecting these treasures, we ensure that future generations can also learn from them. Whether you are an art historian, a casual tourist, or a student, Ravenna offers something for everyone. Its UNESCO status guarantees international support for ongoing conservation. The city’s vibrant cultural calendar keeps the ancient legacy alive and relevant. Plan your trip to Ravenna during spring or autumn for comfortable weather and fewer crowds. Early morning visits to the basilicas allow you to enjoy the mosaics in tranquil light. Bring a notebook to sketch details that may inspire your own creative projects. Finally, take a moment to sit quietly in one of the courtyard gardens and contemplate the same stones that have witnessed history for over fifteen hundred years. Ravenna’s Byzantine mosaics are not only works of art; they are windows into a world where faith, power, and beauty intersected to shape a lasting cultural heritage.

An integral-based method for identifying fourth‑order geodesic invariants in stationary, axisymmetric vacuum spacetimes

Abstract
We present a novel integral formulation for constructing fourth‑order constants of motion associated with geodesic motion in stationary, axisymmetric vacuum spacetimes. The method relies on volume integrals of Killing‑tensor candidates derived from the metric’s Ernst potential. By imposing divergence‑free conditions on appropriate tensorial currents, we obtain algebraic constraints that select admissible fourth‑order invariants. The approach is demonstrated on the Kerr metric and a family of deformed Kerr solutions, confirming known results and revealing new invariants in non‑Kerr geometries. Our findings suggest a systematic pathway for extending integrability analyses beyond quadratic order.

1. Introduction
Geodesic motion in general relativity is governed by the spacetime metric, and its integrability depends on the existence of conserved quantities. In stationary, axisymmetric vacuum spacetimes, two obvious invariants are the energy and the axial component of angular momentum, both arising from Killing vectors. For the Kerr solution an additional quadratic invariant, the Carter constant, derives from a rank‑2 Killing tensor, rendering the geodesic equations completely integrable. However, for more general axisymmetric metrics, higher‑order invariants may exist, and their identification is essential for understanding particle dynamics, gravitational wave emission, and shadow formation. Previous attempts to find such invariants relied on solving Killing‑tensor equations directly, a procedure that rapidly becomes intractable for tensors of rank three or higher. Alternative strategies have employed symmetry operators or perturbative expansions, yet a unified and computationally tractable method remains lacking.

In this work we propose an integral‑based technique that converts the differential Killing‑tensor equations into volume‑integral constraints. By constructing divergence‑free currents from candidate tensors and integrating over a spatial hypersurface, we turn the problem into an algebraic one. This approach parallels the use of Komar integrals for Killing vectors but is extended to higher rank. The central hypothesis is that any genuine fourth‑order invariant must be associated with a totally symmetric, rank‑4 Killing tensor that satisfies a generalized Killing equation. When contracted twice with the four‑velocity, this tensor yields a scalar conserved along geodesics.

2. Mathematical Preliminaries
We consider a four‑dimensional Lorentzian manifold (M,g) solving the vacuum Einstein equations, admitting two commuting Killing vectors ξ( t) = ∂ t and ξ( φ) = ∂ φ . In adapted coordinates (t, r, θ, φ) the metric can be expressed through the Ernst potential E(r,θ), satisfying the Ernst equation. The stationary‑axisymmetric line element assumes the Papapetrou form
ds² = −f(dt−ω dφ)² + f⁻¹[ e2γ (dr² + r² dθ²) + r² sin²θ dφ² ],
where f, ω and γ are functions of (r,θ). The geodesic equations follow from the Lagrangian L = (1/2) g μν ẋ μ ẋ ν . Constants of motion arise from contractions of the four‑velocity u⁰ with Killing tensors K^{(p)} of rank p, defined by the symmetrized covariant derivative ∇_(α K_{βγδ)} = 0 for p = 4.

The divergence‑free current associated with a symmetric tensor T^{μνρσ} and a vector field v⁡α is J^μ = T^{μνρσ} v_ν v_ρ v_σ . Its covariant divergence vanishes if T satisfies the Killing‑tensor condition and v is a geodesic tangent. Integration of ∇_μ J^μ over a region Ω yields, by Stokes’ theorem, a surface integral that must vanish for any closed boundary, providing global constraints on T.

3. Construction of the Integral Constraints
We begin by positing a general ansatz for a rank‑4 symmetric tensor built from the metric, the Killing vectors, and the Levi‑Civita tensor ε_{μναβ}. The most general linear combination involves scalar functions A_i(r,θ) multiplying basis tensors formed from products of ξ(t), ξ(φ), the metric g, and ε. Explicitly,
K_{μνρσ} = A_1 g_{(μν} g_{ρσ)} + A_2 ξ_{(μ} ξ_ν g_{ρσ)} + A_3 ξ_{(μ} ξ_ν ξ_ρ ξ_{σ)} + A_4 ε_{α(μν} ε^{α}_{\ ρσ)} .
The symmetrization ensures total symmetry.

We then define the current J^μ = K^{μνρσ} u_ν u_ρ u_σ, where u is the tangent to a timelike geodesic. The divergence ∇_μ J^μ can be expressed in terms of derivatives of the functions A_i and the metric coefficients. Imposing ∇_μ J^μ = 0 for arbitrary geodesics yields a set of partial differential equations for the A_i. Instead of solving them pointwise, we integrate over a hypersurface Σ of constant t extending from the horizon to spatial infinity. The volume element is √h d³x with h the induced metric on Σ.

The integrated condition ∫_Σ ∇_μ J^μ √h d³x = 0 reduces, by Gauss’s theorem, to a surface integral at infinity and at the horizon. Assuming asymptotic flatness and regularity at the horizon, the surface contributions vanish, leaving
∫_Σ (∇_μ J^μ) √h d³x = 0.
Substituting the explicit form of ∇_μ J^μ, the integral becomes a bilinear functional of the functions A_i and their gradients. Because the integrand is a sum of products of independent angular functions (e.g., Legendre polynomials), the integral separates into independent equations for each angular mode. This yields a finite system of ordinary differential equations in r for the radial parts of A_i.

4. Solving the Reduced System
We solve the reduced ODE system by series expansion in 1/r for large r, matching coefficients to enforce asymptotic flatness. The leading terms fix A_1 = const, corresponding to the trivial invariant built from the metric itself. The next orders constrain A_2 and A_3, revealing that nontrivial fourth‑order invariants can exist only if the metric functions f and ω satisfy specific relations. For the Kerr metric these relations are automatically satisfied, reproducing the known quartic invariant associated with the hidden symmetry generated by the Killing‑Yano tensor. For deformed Kerr spacetimes with quadrupole perturbations, the constraints impose conditions on the perturbation parameters; only a subset of deformations admit a fourth‑order invariant.

We implement the ODE system numerically for a family of metrics parameterized by a deformation parameter δ, representing deviations from Kerr quadrupole moment. By scanning δ we locate a narrow interval where the integral constraints admit solutions, indicating the persistence of a fourth‑order invariant. Outside this interval the constraints are inconsistent, confirming the loss of integrability.

5. Examples and Verification
First, we apply the method to the Kerr metric with mass M and spin a. The Ernst potential reduces to E = (r - i a cosθ)/(r + i a cosθ). Substituting into the integral equations yields A_1 = 1, A_2 = 0, A_3 = (a²/M⁴), and A_4 = 0, reproducing the known quartic invariant K_{μνρσ} u^μ u^ν u^ρ u^σ = (Carter constant)². Direct evaluation of J^μ confirms ∇_μ J^μ = 0 analytically.

Second, we consider the Manko–Novikov metric, which introduces higher multipole moments while preserving stationarity and axisymmetry. The integral constraints become highly restrictive; only when the multipole coefficients satisfy a specific algebraic relation does a solution for A_i exist. This relation coincides with the condition for the existence of a fourth‑order Killing tensor reported in earlier literature, providing an independent verification of our method.

Third, we test a toy metric with a simple quadrupole deformation: f = 1 - 2M/r + q (M³/r³) P₂(cosθ), ω = 2aM r sin²θ/(r² + a² cos²θ), where q is a dimensionless quadrupole parameter. Numerical integration of the constraints shows that a fourth‑order invariant exists for q = 0 (Kerr) and for q ≈ 0.12 within numerical tolerance, suggesting a previously unnoticed integrable deformation.

6. Discussion
The integral‑based approach circumvents the complexity of directly solving the Killing‑tensor equations by converting them into global constraints that are amenable to analytic and numeric treatment. The method exploits the divergence‑free property of currents built from candidate tensors, a feature shared by Komar integrals for Killing vectors. Its success in reproducing known invariants for Kerr validates the formalism, while the discovery of permissible deformations indicates its potential for uncovering new integrable spacetimes.

One limitation is the reliance on asymptotic flatness and regular horizons to eliminate surface terms. In spacetimes with cosmological constant or without horizons, additional boundary contributions must be accounted for, possibly leading to modified constraints. Moreover, the ansatz for K_{μνρσ} was restricted to low‑order polynomial combinations of the basic geometric objects; more exotic tensors may require extensions of the basis.

The technique also suggests a hierarchy: starting from rank‑2 Killing tensors one can construct rank‑4 candidates by tensor products, while ensuring that the resulting currents remain divergence‑free. This hierarchy may be explored to generate systematic families of higher‑order invariants.

7. Conclusions
We have introduced an integral‑based method for the identification of fourth‑order geodesic invariants in stationary, axisymmetric vacuum spacetimes. By formulating divergence‑free currents from a general symmetric rank‑4 tensor and integrating over a spatial hypersurface, we derived algebraic and ordinary differential constraints on the tensor components. Application to Kerr and deformed Kerr metrics confirmed known results and revealed new admissible deformations supporting a quartic invariant. The method offers a practical tool for probing integrability in a broad class of spacetimes and may be extended to higher rank invariants and to spacetimes with different asymptotics.

Ethan walked the hallway alone, his shoulders hunched against the whispers that followed him. Every day, the same taunts echoed off the lockers, a chorus of cruelty that seemed to grow louder each morning. He tried to ignore the jeers, but they carved deep grooves in his confidence. At lunch, he sat at the end of the cafeteria, a lone chair his sanctuary and his prison. The other kids never invited him to join their games, their laughter a reminder of the space he could not fill. One afternoon, after a particularly harsh shove, Ethan's notebook fell open, spilling ink‑stained pages across the floor. Among the scribbles was a sketch of a dragon, its wings spread wide, breathing fire. He stared at the drawing, feeling a strange flicker of pride. The dragon, unlike him, was powerful and feared. In that moment, Ethan wondered what it would be like to be fearless. He took the broken pieces of his self‑esteem and began to collect them like puzzle fragments. Each night, he practiced drawing, each stroke a small rebellion against the mockery he endured. His art became a secret language, a way to speak without words. He started to stay after school in the art room, where the fluorescent lights hummed softly. The teacher, Ms. Rivera, noticed his talent and encouraged him to enter the upcoming school art showcase. Ethan hesitated, his mind crowded with doubts. “What if they laugh at my work?” he whispered to himself. Ms. Rivera smiled and said, “Sometimes the best way to silence the noise is to let your voice shine through the colors.” Encouraged, Ethan submitted his dragon sketch, along with a new piece—a portrait of a boy with closed eyes, his heart visible as a glow. The day of the showcase arrived, and the gym was filled with displays of paint, clay, and photographs. Ethan’s drawings hung at eye level, quiet and waiting. Students drifted past, some snickering, some indifferent, but a few lingered, drawn to the intensity of his lines. Among the lingering crowd stood Maya, a quiet girl from his science class who often kept to herself. She stared at the dragon, then at the glowing heart, and felt something stir inside her. “It’s beautiful,” she said softly, surprising herself with the words. Ethan turned, startled, his throat tight. “Thanks,” he replied, the word feeling both foreign and relieving. Maya nodded and moved on, but she returned later, standing beside his work again. “I draw too,” she confessed, pulling a small sketchbook from her backpack. Inside were delicate ink drawings of constellations and tiny planets. “I feel safe looking at stars,” she said. Ethan smiled, a genuine lift of his lips. They talked about lines and shadows, about how art could hide pain and also expose truth. For the first time, Ethan felt the weight of his loneliness lighten, replaced by a thread of connection. The next day, Maya invited him to sit with her during lunch, a small act that felt monumental. Ethan accepted, his heart beating faster than usual. As they ate, Maya shared stories of her own bullying, of whispers that called her “odd.” Ethan listened, realizing his struggle was not unique. He opened up about the dragon, about how he wished he could breathe fire to scare off his tormentors. Maya laughed, a soft sound that seemed to melt the ice around his throat. “You don’t need fire,” she said, “you already have a fire inside you.” Their conversation drifted to favorite books, music, and the secret places they imagined escaping to. By the end of lunch, Ethan felt a warmth he had not known for years. The bullying did not vanish overnight, but the sting dulled with each shared smile. He began to notice small gestures of kindness from classmates he had never spoken to before. One boy, Jake, offered to carry his locker books without a word of ridicule. Ethan thanked him, surprised by the sincerity in Jake’s eyes. The next week, Jake joined Ethan and Maya at the art room after school, eager to learn drawing techniques. Their trio grew, and with each meeting, Ethan’s confidence thickened like paint on a canvas. He started to speak up in class, his voice steadier when answering questions. The teachers noticed the change, praising his participation. At home, Ethan’s mother saw the shift and encouraged him to keep creating. “Your art shows how brave you are,” she told him, hugging him tightly. With each affirmation, the shadows of his past receded. One rainy afternoon, the school announced a talent show, inviting performances of any kind. Ethan felt a spark of excitement and fear intertwine. He considered entering, but the idea of standing on stage terrified him. Maya nudged him gently, “What if you read your poem? It’s about the dragon, right?” He had written a poem about the dragon’s journey, about overcoming fear. After much deliberation, Ethan agreed to perform. He practiced in front of the mirror, stumbling over lines until they felt natural. On the night of the talent show, the auditorium buzzed with anticipation. Ethan waited backstage, heart thudding like a drum. He saw the faces of his former bullies in the crowd, their eyes curious. He inhaled, recalling Maya’s words about his inner fire. When his name was called, he stepped onto the stage, the lights blinding him for a moment. He cleared his throat and began to read, his voice trembling at first. As he spoke of a dragon that learned to let down its guard, his words gained strength. The audience fell silent, listening to the vulnerability woven into his verses. When he finished, a ripple of applause rose, genuine and warm. Even the boys who once mocked him clapped, some with a hint of remorse in their eyes. Ethan felt a tear escape, not of sadness but of relief. After the show, Maya rushed to his side, hugging him tightly. “You were amazing,” she whispered, eyes shining. One of the former bullies, Ryan, approached hesitantly. “I… I didn’t realize how you felt,” he said, voice low. Ethan looked at him, noticing the uncertainty in his gaze. “It’s okay,” Ethan replied, “We can all start over.” Ryan nodded, and the two exchanged a brief, tentative handshake. From that night onward, the hallway dynamics shifted subtly. Ethan no longer walked alone; he walked with friends who understood his scars. He still felt moments of doubt, but they no longer controlled him. He continued to draw, his art now filled with bright colors and open skies. Maya’s constellations appeared alongside his dragons, forming new stories. The school held an exhibition of student art, featuring Ethan’s pieces prominently. Parents and teachers praised his evolution, citing his bravery as an example. Ethan stood before a crowd, accepting a small award, his speech brief but heartfelt. “I learned that being vulnerable is not a weakness,” he said, “it is the bridge to real connection.” The applause echoed, a sound that felt like affirmation. After the ceremony, Jake offered to collaborate on a mural for the school’s front wall. Together, they designed a massive canvas depicting a dragon soaring above a city of diverse faces. The project brought many students together, painting side by side. As they worked, jokes were shared, paint splattered, and old grudges faded. Ethan realized that reconciliation did not erase the past, but transformed it into something constructive. He often thought back to the broken notebook that started it all, grateful for the chance to rebuild. Years later, he returned to the school as a guest speaker, speaking to a new generation of students. He told them about the power of art, vulnerability, and the courage to ask for help. The audience listened, some with eyes wet, others with inspired smiles. After his talk, a shy boy approached, clutching a sketchpad. “Can you give me some advice?” the boy asked, voice trembling. Ethan knelt, opened the boy’s book, and began to point out the hidden sparks of potential, just as someone had once done for him. In that moment, Ethan understood that his transformation was not an endpoint but a continuous loop of giving and receiving, a friendship forged through the simple act of being seen.

Mara watched the quiet town from the hill, convinced its residents were content. She labeled them as complacent, never questioning their simple routines. One stormy night, the power failed and the town plunged into darkness. Mara’s car stalled on the road, forcing her to seek shelter. She knocked on the first door she found, a modest cottage. An elderly man named Eli opened, his eyes weary yet kind. “Come in,” he said, “the rain is fierce.” Inside, Mara felt the heat of a wood stove and the scent of stew. She noticed a wall lined with photographs of lost loved ones. “We’ve had our share of grief,” Eli whispered. Mara sensed a heaviness she had never imagined. The next morning, the town’s main street was flooded. Shops were closed, and the baker’s windows were cracked. Mara joined volunteers, pulling sandbags with strangers she once mocked. She learned that the baker, Tomas, had lost his wife to illness months before. His brief smile hid a deep ache that never fully healed. At the community center, a teenager named Lena paced restlessly. Lena confessed she felt trapped by expectations of her family. Mara realized the pressure of conformity was a silent burden. The floodwaters receded, leaving mud and debris in their wake. The town organized a clean‑up, and Mara scrubbed sidewalks beside Eli. He told stories of wars he survived as a boy. Mara listened, feeling the weight of sacrifices she’d dismissed. That evening, the town gathered around a bonfire. Music rose, and people danced despite the lingering chill. Mara saw a mother cradle her infant, eyes trembling with hope. The mother, Sara, whispered prayers for a better future. Mara understood that hope was a daily struggle, not a given. Days turned into weeks, and the town began to rebuild. New houses rose where old ones had fallen. Mira, a teenage girl, taught children to read under a battered awning. Her patience revealed the value of education in hardship. Mara helped paint a mural on the town hall’s side. The mural depicted hands reaching across a river, symbolizing unity. As she painted, she recalled her earlier judgments. She felt shame for her arrogance. The mayor, Carlos, approached and thanked her sincerely. He shared how the town’s budget had been slashed years ago. The residents had survived on barter and mutual aid. Mara realized that financial security was a fragile illusion. One night, a fire broke out in the barn. Smoke billowed, and panic spread. The townspeople formed a bucket chain, fighting the flames together. Mara carried a bucket, her arms burning from effort. When the fire died, the barn was charred but not destroyed. The farmers salvaged what they could, grateful for every grain. Eli smiled, his eyes shining with pride. “You belong now,” he said. Mara felt a belonging she never expected. She began to write letters to her distant friends. In them, she described the resilience she witnessed. Her friends read with disbelief, then curiosity. They asked why she had left her city life. “Because I needed to see truth,” she replied. Winter arrived, blanketing the town in white. The school closed, and children played in the snow. Mara learned to ice‑fish with Tomas, his hands steady despite age. He taught her patience, waiting for a bite that might never come. The silence of the lake mirrored her thoughts. She thought of the judgments she’d made. Their echo faded as she pulled a glistening fish from the water. Tomas laughed, “Even in stillness, life moves.” At the church, the pastor delivered a sermon on compassion. He quoted a verse about judging not lest we be judged. The congregation nodded, feeling the truth in his words. After service, Mara approached the pastor. He asked her what she sought. “Understanding,” she whispered. He handed her a small notebook, urging her to record her experiences. Mara filled pages with names, faces, and emotions. She discovered that each person carried invisible scars. The scars were not always visible, but they shaped actions. One afternoon, a stray dog appeared at the market. Children chased it, fearing it might bite. Sara coaxed the dog with gentle words, earning its trust. The dog, named Hope, followed her home. Hope became a symbol of the town’s perseverance. Mara adopted the dog, feeling its warm presence each night. In spring, the town held a festival of blossoms. Flowers covered the streets, bright against the lingering mud. Music floated, and laughter echoed from every corner. Mara danced with Lina, their shoes splashing in puddles of rainwater. The dance reminded her of life’s unpredictable rhythm. At the festival’s end, a thunderstorm rolled in unexpectedly. The crowd hurried for shelter, but no panic arose. They shared umbrellas, huddling together under one large tarp. Mare’s heart swelled with gratitude for their solidarity. The storm passed, leaving rainbows arching across the sky. That night, Mara sat on her porch, reflecting. She realized judgment had blinded her to humanity’s shared pain. The wind whispered through the trees, carrying stories of old. She felt humbled by the depth of each story. The next day, she organized a storytelling night. Residents gathered around lanterns, sharing tales of loss and love. Eli recounted his escape from a war‑torn village. Lena spoke about her dream to become an artist. Tomas revealed his secret recipe for bread, learned from his mother. Sara sang a lullaby her grandmother taught her. The night stitched the community tighter than before. Mara wrote a final entry in her notebook. She described how judgment had been a shield she no longer needed. The shield had cracked, allowing empathy to flood in. As she closed the notebook, she felt peace. The town’s bell rang, marking midnight. Its chime resonated through the valley, a reminder of time’s flow. Mara stepped into the street, breathing the crisp air. She saw the sunrise paint the roofs gold. The day promised new challenges, but also hope. She whispered to Hope, “We walk this road together.” The dog wagged, his tail a metronome of content. Eli waved from his porch, a silent salute. Tomas handed her a loaf, warm and fragrant. Lena handed her a sketch of the hill, lines bold and sure. Sara offered a hand‑woven scarf, colors bright. Each gift represented a lesson learned. Mara accepted them, feeling their weight and meaning. She realized that lives once judged were complex tapestries. Every thread intertwined with loss, joy, and perseverance. The town’s rhythm pulsed beneath her feet. She no longer stood apart as an observer. She became part of the story, living its verses. Days turned into years, and the town flourished. New families arrived, bringing fresh perspectives. Mara welcomed them, remembering her own arrival. She taught them to listen before forming opinions. The cycle of judgment broke, replaced by understanding. The hill that once seemed distant now felt like home. Mara smiled, knowing that empathy had healed both her and the town. And in that quiet valley, the echoes of past judgments faded into songs of unity.

Dr. Elias Marlowe had spent three decades chasing the lost city of Aramith. His colleagues admired his relentless devotion. He believed the ancient civilization held the key to humanity’s origins. One rainy afternoon, a small crate arrived at his university office. Inside was a tarnished bronze ring inscribed with unknown glyphs. The package bore a single note: “For the seeker who dares.” Curiosity overrode caution, and Elias slipped the ring onto his finger. A shiver ran up his arm, and the world seemed to tilt. The ring pulsed with a cold fire that only he could feel. In that moment, a whisper brushed his mind: “You will find what you seek, but not what you need.” He laughed nervously, dismissing it as imagination. Yet the next day, his grant applications were mysteriously denied. A rival professor published a paper preemptively on Aramith’s architecture. Funding agencies called his research “obsolete.” The ring grew heavier with each setback. Elias found himself obsessively polishing the artifact instead of planning expeditions. He stopped teaching his graduate students, who whispered about his change. His wife, Mara, tried to intervene, but he brushed her concerns aside. “It’s just a phase,” he told her, though his voice trembled. The ring seemed to whisper louder each night. It promised visions of buried temples and golden sigils. Sleep evaded him, replaced by feverish dreams of sand and stone. One dawn, he packed a rucksack, abandoning his apartment keys. He boarded a cargo ship bound for the coast of Turkmenistan, where rumors placed Aramith’s entrance. The crew eyed his gaunt appearance with suspicion. He kept the ring hidden under a cloth, feeling its weight like a secret heartbeat. Upon disembarking, a local guide named Karim approached him. Karim offered his services for a modest fee, sensing Elias’s desperation. Together they trekked across a blistering desert, the ring’s cold biting his skin. Days turned into weeks as they followed fragmented maps. The ring guided them, pointing toward hidden valleys with a faint glow. Finally, they stood before a yawning stone doorway, half-buried in dunes. Elias felt triumphant, yet an unsettling dread washed over him. He entered, and the air grew thick with ancient incense. Inside, murals depicted a king wearing a ring identical to Elias’s. The inscription matched the glyphs on his band. A sudden tremor cracked the floor, and a hidden chamber opened. The darkness seemed to swallow his torch’s light. He heard a low chant emanating from the walls. Shadows coalesced into a spectral figure, a priestess draped in silver. “You have awakened the curse,” she intoned, her voice echoing. “The ring binds the seeker to the past, stealing his present.” Elias tried to reason, but his tongue felt glued. The priestess raised a hand, and the ring flared with blinding light. In that flash, memories of Mara’s smile, his daughter’s laughter, and his students’ hopeful eyes flooded him. The curse’s purpose became clear: it fed on his isolation. The ring had drawn him away from love to satisfy its own hunger. With a surge of will, Elias ripped the ring off his finger. It fell to the stone, shattering into a cascade of cold sparks. The spectral priestess dissolved, leaving a whisper: “Return to those who love you.” Elias staggered out of the chamber, his heart pounding. Karim looked at him, concern etched on his weathered face. “You’re alive,” he said, offering water. Elias realized he had been gone for months, his absence unnoticed in the world above. He thanked Karim and began the long trek back to civilization. The desert seemed less hostile now that his purpose shifted. When he finally reached the coastal town, a message awaited him. Mara stood on the pier, holding his daughter, Lila, in her arms. Tears streamed down their faces as they ran to embrace him. “We thought you’d never return,” Mara whispered, clutching his hand. Lila giggled, tugging at his shirt, “Daddy, you’re home!” The reunion ignited a warmth that melted the remnants of the ring’s chill. Karim bowed, offering a simple gift: a palm leaf inscribed with protective symbols. “Take this,” he said, “to guard against lingering shadows.” Elias accepted, feeling gratitude swell within him. Back at the university, he resumed his lectures with renewed vigor. He shared his experience without revealing the cursed ring, speaking of balance between past and present. His students listened, inspired by his humility. The department reinstated his grant, impressed by his recent fieldwork. Mara returned to her art studio, painting vibrant scenes of desert sunsets. Lila began studying archaeology, eager to follow in her father’s footsteps. Together, the family often visited museums, their bond strengthening. Karim visited occasionally, bringing exotic spices and stories. One evening, they gathered around a fire, laughing as Lila attempted to translate ancient scripts. Elias watched, realizing his true mission had always been about connection, not just discovery. He understood that knowledge meant little without someone to share it with. The curse had taught him that obsession blinds the heart. He vowed never again to let a singular focus eclipse his relationships. Months turned into years, and the Aramith project progressed under a collaborative team. They uncovered a library of clay tablets, revealing a philosophy of communal stewardship. Elias published a groundbreaking paper, crediting his team and his family’s support. He received an award for lifetime achievement, which he accepted on stage with Mara beside him. In his acceptance speech, he spoke of the ring that had nearly cost him everything. He thanked the unseen forces that reminded him of love’s power. The audience rose in a standing ovation, moved by his honesty. After the ceremony, Lila presented him with a necklace she had crafted, shaped like a tiny ring. “A symbol of balance,” she said, smiling. He placed it over his heart, feeling its gentle weight. It served as a reminder that purpose flourishes when rooted in family. Years later, when the sun set over the desert, Elias would walk with Mara hand in hand. They would point to distant dunes and recall the night the cursed ring changed everything. Their love grew richer with each shared memory. Lila, now a professor, guided a new generation of seekers. Karim retired to a quiet village, his name spoken reverently among locals. The palm leaf symbol he gave Elias was framed in the department’s hallway. Visitors marveled at its intricate design, unaware of its protective origin. The cursed ring lay shattered in a forgotten tomb, its fragments inert. No longer a threat, it became a relic of caution for future explorers. Elias often taught his students to heed the lessons of humility. He emphasized that ambition without compassion leads to emptiness. The story of the cursed ring circulated as a legend among archaeologists. It reminded them that the greatest discoveries are those made within the heart. In quiet moments, Elias would close his eyes and feel Mara’s breath beside him. He thanked the universe for the second chance he had been given. And he vowed to honor that gift by living fully, with love as his compass. The desert wind whispered, carrying his promise across the sands forever.

Longitudinal NMR Analysis of Urinary Metabolites to Track Methylmalonic Aciduria, Treatment Effects, and Mutation‑Related Differences

Abstract  
Methylmalonic aciduria (MMA) comprises a heterogeneous group of inherited metabolic disorders characterized by the accumulation of methylmalonic acid (MMA) and related metabolites. Early diagnosis and continuous monitoring are essential to mitigate neurologic damage and metabolic decompensation. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy offers a non‑invasive, quantitative approach for profiling urinary metabolites over time. In this study we performed serial ^1H‑NMR metabolomics on urine samples from a cohort of 68 patients with genetically confirmed MMA, followed for a median of 4.2 years. We evaluated metabolite trajectories, treatment responses to cobalamin, carnitine, and dietary protein restriction, and examined the influence of underlying mutational subtypes (mut0, mut‑, cblA, cblB, cblC, and cblD). Multivariate statistical models identified a panel of ten metabolites that reliably discriminated disease activity and therapeutic effect. Moreover, mutation‑specific metabolic signatures were uncovered, suggesting distinct biochemical pathways perturbed by each genotype. Our findings demonstrate that longitudinal urinary NMR profiling is a powerful tool for personalized management of MMA and for elucidating genotype‑phenotype relationships.

Keywords  
Methylmalonic aciduria, urinary metabolomics, ^1H‑NMR spectroscopy, longitudinal study, genotype‑phenotype correlation, metabolic therapy.

1. Introduction  
Methylmalonic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting from defects in the conversion of methylmalonyl‑CoA to succinyl‑CoA. The most common genetic causes are mutations in the genes encoding methylmalonyl‑CoA mutase (MUT) and the enzymes required for its cofactor synthesis (cblA, cblB, cblC, cblD). Clinical presentation ranges from severe neonatal crisis to milder late‑onset forms. Accumulation of MMA, propionyl‑CoA‑derived metabolites, and secondary disturbances such as hyperammonemia drive the pathology.

Current monitoring relies on periodic measurement of plasma MMA, plasma amino acids, and clinical assessment, but these parameters provide limited insight into dynamic metabolic adaptation. Urine, being a rich reservoir of excreted metabolites, reflects systemic metabolic fluxes and can be sampled repeatedly with minimal burden. ^1H‑NMR spectroscopy enables untargeted detection of metabolites at concentrations from micromolar to millimolar, offering a comprehensive metabolic snapshot. Prior cross‑sectional studies have described urinary metabolic profiles of MMA patients, yet the temporal evolution of these profiles under treatment remains poorly defined.

The objective of this study was to conduct a longitudinal NMR‑based metabolomic analysis of urine from patients with MMA, to (i) characterize metabolite trajectories over time, (ii) assess the metabolic impact of standard therapies, and (iii) identify mutation‑specific metabolic signatures. We hypothesized that (a) recurrent NMR measurements would capture fluctuations in disease activity, (b) treatment would induce characteristic shifts in metabolite concentrations, and (c) different genetic subtypes would display distinct metabolic fingerprints.

2. Materials and Methods  

2.1. Study Population  
We recruited 68 patients (38 males, 30 females) from three metabolic centers in Europe and North America between 2018 and 2025. Inclusion criteria required a biochemical diagnosis of MMA (plasma MMA > 250 µmol/L) and confirmation of pathogenic mutations by Sanger sequencing or next‑generation panel. Patients were classified according to genotype: mut0 (n = 12), mut‑ (n = 10), cblA (n = 14), cblB (n = 11), cblC (n = 9), and cblD (n = 12). Age at enrollment ranged from 2 months to 16 years (median 3.4 years). All participants or guardians gave informed consent; the protocol was approved by local ethics committees.

2.2. Clinical Management  
Standard care included hydroxocobalamin (10–20 mg IM weekly for cblA/cblB, higher for MUT deficiency), oral L‑carnitine (100 mg/kg/day), and individualized protein restriction (0.8–1.2 g/kg/day). Patients with severe mut0 disease also received renal transplantation in 5 cases. Clinical data (growth parameters, neurodevelopmental scores, frequency of metabolic decompensation) were recorded at each visit.

2.3. Sample Collection and Processing  
Urine was collected in sterile containers at baseline and then every three months for up to 5 years. Samples were stored at –80 °C within 2 h of collection. Prior to NMR, urine was thawed on ice, centrifuged at 12 000 g for 10 min, and mixed with phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) containing 0.1 % sodium azide and 10 % D_2O. An internal standard (0.5 mM TSP) was added for chemical shift referencing.

2.4. NMR Acquisition  
Spectra were recorded on a 600 MHz Bruker Avance III spectrometer equipped with a cryoprobe. For each sample, a standard one‑dimensional NOESY presaturation pulse sequence was used (64 k points, 128 scans, relaxation delay 4 s). Water suppression was achieved via presaturation. Spectra were Fourier transformed, phased, baseline corrected, and referenced to TSP at 0.00 ppm using TopSpin software.

2.5. Data Pre‑processing  
Spectral regions containing residual water (4.5–5.0 ppm) and urea (5.6–5.8 ppm) were excluded. Remaining data were reduced to 0.01 ppm buckets, normalized to the total spectral area, and log‑transformed. Metabolite identification was performed by comparison with reference libraries (Human Metabolome Database, Chenomx) and confirmed by spiking experiments for key metabolites (MMA, 2‑methylcitrate, propionate, glycine, alanine, succinate, formate, hippurate, citrate, and creatinine).

2.6. Statistical Analyses  
Longitudinal data were analyzed using linear mixed‑effects models (LME) with random intercepts for each patient, fixed effects for time, treatment variables, and genotype. The primary outcome was the concentration of MMA; secondary outcomes were the concentrations of the nine additional metabolites identified. False discovery rate (FDR) correction (Benjamini‑Hochberg) was applied for multiple testing. Principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS‑DA) were employed to visualize group separation. Model performance was evaluated by cross‑validation (7‑fold) and external validation on a held‑out subset (15 % of samples). All analyses were conducted in R (v4.4) using nlme, mixOmics, and caret packages.

3. Results  

3.1. Cohort Characteristics  
The median follow‑up duration was 4.2 years (range 1.0–5.0 years). During the study, 23 metabolic decompensation episodes were recorded, all occurring in the first 12 months after enrollment. Growth velocity improved in 54 % of patients receiving combined hydroxocobalamin and carnitine therapy. Neurodevelopmental scores (Bayley‑III) increased modestly in the cblA and cblB subgroups but remained stable in mut0 patients.

3.2. Baseline Urinary Metabolome  
At baseline, urinary MMA concentrations varied widely (median 12.8 mmol/mol creatinine, interquartile range 5.3–22.4). The mut0 group displayed the highest median MMA (19.2 mmol/mol), whereas cblC patients had lower values (7.1 mmol/mol). In addition to MMA, elevated levels of 2‑methylcitrate, propionate, and succinate were observed across all genotypes, with the greatest perturbations in mut0 and mut‑ patients.

3.3. Longitudinal Trajectories of MMA  
LME analysis revealed a significant time‑by‑treatment interaction (p < 0.001). Patients receiving weekly hydroxocobalamin demonstrated a mean annual MMA reduction of 1.8 mmol/mol (95 % CI −2.3 to −1.3). In contrast, patients on low‑dose oral cyanocobalamin showed no significant change (p = 0.42). The addition of L‑carnitine yielded an extra 0.6 mmol/mol annual decrease (p = 0.02). A genotype‑specific pattern emerged: cblA and cblB subgroups responded more robustly to hydroxocobalamin (average 2.4 mmol/mol/year) than mut0 patients (0.9 mmol/mol/year).

3.4. Multivariate Metabolic Shifts  
PCA of all urinary spectra demonstrated a clear separation between baseline and 24‑month samples (PC1 explained 38 % of variance). OPLS‑DA models discriminating treated versus untreated states achieved an accuracy of 0.87 (95 % CI 0.81–0.92) and identified a panel of ten metabolites with high variable importance: MMA, 2‑methylcitrate, propionate, glycine, alanine, succinate, formate, hippurate, citrate, and creatinine. The loadings indicated that treatment primarily reduced MMA, 2‑methylcitrate, and propionate, while increasing glycine and hippurate.

3.5. Mutation‑Related Metabolic Signatures  
Genotype‑specific OPLS‑DA models yielded distinct metabolic fingerprints. mut0 patients exhibited persistently high MMA and 2‑methylcitrate, coupled with low glycine and elevated succinate. cblA patients showed moderate MMA reduction but a pronounced increase in hippurate and formate, suggesting enhanced hepatic detoxification. cblC patients displayed an unusual accumulation of methylmalonate‑derived N‑acetylated compounds, not observed in other groups. Cross‑validation confirmed that genotype could be predicted from urinary metabolite profiles with an overall accuracy of 0.81.

3.6. Clinical Correlations  
Higher urinary MMA levels were strongly associated with the frequency of metabolic crises (Spearman ρ = 0.68, p < 0.001). In multivariate models, improvements in growth velocity correlated with reductions in both MMA and propionate (β = 0.24, p = 0.004). Neurodevelopmental gains were linked to increased hippurate and formate, metabolites known to reflect gut microbiota activity, suggesting a possible ancillary role of microbiome modulation.

3.7. Validation in an Independent Cohort  
An external validation cohort of 15 MMA patients (different centers, same inclusion criteria) was analyzed using the same NMR pipeline. The ten‑metabolite panel predicted treatment response with sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.79, confirming the robustness of the biomarkers.

4. Discussion  

4.1. Summary of Findings  
Our longitudinal NMR study demonstrates that urinary metabolite profiling can sensitively track disease activity in MMA, distinguish therapeutic effects, and reveal genotype‑specific metabolic patterns. The identified ten‑metabolite panel offers a practical set of biomarkers for routine monitoring.

4.2. Comparison with Prior Work  
Previous cross‑sectional metabolomic reports identified MMA and 2‑methylcitrate as hallmark urinary metabolites, but they lacked temporal resolution. Our data extend these observations by quantifying the rate of metabolic change under therapy and by uncovering additional metabolites (hippurate, formate) that respond to treatment and correlate with clinical outcomes.

4.3. Biological Implications  
The persistent elevation of succinate in mut0 patients may reflect downstream blockade of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, while the rise in hippurate and formate in cblA/B suggests compensatory activation of gut‑liver detox pathways. The distinct N‑acetylated metabolite accumulation in cblC points to impaired methylation capacity beyond cobalamin metabolism.

4.4. Clinical Utility  
Routine urinary NMR could complement plasma MMA measurements, offering a non‑invasive, high‑throughput tool for personalized treatment adjustment. For instance, patients whose urinary MMA fails to decline despite cobalamin supplementation may be candidates for liver transplantation or gene therapy trials.

4.5. Limitations  
The study cohort, though multinational, was limited in size for rare genotypes such as cblD, reducing statistical power for those subgroups. Dietary intake was not tightly controlled, which may confound some metabolite variations. Additionally, NMR resolution does not allow differentiation of isomeric compounds without further chromatographic separation.

4.6. Future Directions  
Integrating urinary NMR with plasma metabolomics and microbiome sequencing could elucidate the inter‑organ metabolic network in MMA. Long‑term follow‑up beyond five years will ascertain whether early metabolic normalization predicts improved adult outcomes. Finally, the identified metabolic signatures could serve as surrogate endpoints in clinical trials of novel enzyme replacement or gene‑editing therapies.

5. Conclusions  
Serial ^1H‑NMR spectroscopy of urine provides a dynamic, quantitative window into the metabolic landscape of methylmalonic aciduria. It captures treatment‑induced metabolic shifts, reveals mutation‑specific biochemical perturbations, and correlates with clinically meaningful endpoints. Adoption of urinary NMR monitoring may enhance personalized care and accelerate therapeutic development for this complex metabolic disorder.
